## Sequence of events (SOE)




- 2025-11-27 evening (CT) TRIGGER On the live approach to a hard freeze in the Chicago suburbs (Thanksgiving-window reopen), onsite staff and contractors began preparing/draining CHI1's cooling towers for freezing weather but failed to follow standard procedures for the winterization changeover (CyrusOne, confirmed to Bloomberg).
- 2025-11-27 evening (CT) CASCADE The procedural lapse induced a chiller-plant failure: CHI1 'experienced a chiller plant failure affecting multiple cooling units' - a common-mode trip taking more than one unit offline at once.
- 2025-11-27 evening (CT) CASCADE Chilled-water circulation to the data halls was lost; against ~109MW of IT capacity with low thermal mass, rack-inlet/room temperatures began climbing (a widely-cited summary reports >100degF; not disclosed by CyrusOne).
- 2025-11-27 late evening (CT) DETECTION Thermal detection (not fire): plant/building monitoring (BMS/DCIM) and rising room/rack temperatures would have driven high-temperature alarms as the chiller plant failed. No accessible source states the exact minute the high-temp threshold tripped.
- 2025-11-27 late evening (ET) MITIGATION Protective compute shutdown: to stop generating heat and protect hardware, CME's trading systems (Globex and related markets) were halted/failed over - an 'evacuation of compute' rather than any occupant evacuation (unmanned mechanical failure, no life-safety event).
- 2025-11-27/28 overnight IMPACT Global markets knocked out: the halt prevented traders from accessing futures prices for commodities and stocks across CME Group's derivatives markets (specific benchmark list per trade reporting: S&P 500, Nasdaq, Treasuries, WTI, gold, Nikkei, palm oil - not independently reconfirmed).
- 2025-11-27/28 overnight MITIGATION CME issued a public notice that its markets were halted due to a cooling issue at the CyrusOne data center and that it was working to resolve the issue (exact wording attributed to trade reporting, not independently reconfirmed).
- 2025-11-27/28 overnight MITIGATION Emergency MECHANICAL response (no fire department / 911): CyrusOne mobilized engineering teams and contractors on-site to restart chillers and reconstitute chilled-water circulation.
- 2025-11-27/28 overnight MITIGATION No suppression discharge occurred or was needed (no fire); the 'suppression analogue' - the cooling plant - had failed. Redundancy/backup cooling did not carry the load, forcing an orderly thermal de-rating/shutdown of IT.
- 2025-11-28 early hours RECOVERY Chillers restarted at limited capacity and cooling reconstituted to rebuild chilled-water circulation to a stable state (any 'temporary/supplemental chillers and pipework' detail is attributed to DC Pulse and is unverified).
- 2025-11-28 ~07:00 ET RECOVERY EBS markets resumed trading as chilled-water circulation stabilized enough to bring IT load back safely (resume time per CNBC; not independently reconfirmed).
- 2025-11-28 ~08:30 ET RESTORED Stock futures and options trading fully reopened; CME reported all its markets were open and trading (per CNBC; not independently reconfirmed).
- 2025-11-28 by ~13:35 GMT RESTORED Trading in FX, stock and bond futures had resumed after being knocked out for roughly/over 11 hours; regulators (CFTC and SEC) reportedly aware and monitoring (per Reuters; not independently reconfirmed).
- 2025-11-28 onward RECOVERY CyrusOne reported it had 'restored stable and secure operations at its Chicago 1 (CHI1) data center in Aurora, Illinois' and 'installed additional redundancy to the cooling systems.'
- 2025-12 (early) IMPACT Financial/reputational fallout: CyrusOne reportedly postponed/halted a bond sale after the data-center failure that disrupted CME, and confirmed to Bloomberg the ~11-hour outage was caused by human error.



## Root cause

 PRIMARY EQUIPMENT / FAILURE MECHANISM. This was a loss-of-cooling (thermal) event, not a fire — no ignition source, no combustion. The failed system was the primary water-cooled CHILLER PLANT serving CyrusOne's CHI1 (Chicago 1 / "CH1") data center in Aurora, Illinois. In CyrusOne's own words the CHI1 facility "experienced a chiller plant failure affecting multiple cooling units" (CyrusOne statement, relayed by DatacenterDynamics). Multiple cooling units dropped offline together, chilled-water circulation to the data halls was lost, and rack-inlet/room temperatures rose until CME Group's trading engines had to be halted to protect hardware.

STATED ROOT CAUSE — HUMAN / PROCEDURAL (CONFIRMED). CyrusOne confirmed to Bloomberg that the ~11-hour outage was caused by human error: onsite staff and contractors failed to follow standard procedures when DRAINING/PREPARING the cooling towers ahead of freezing weather (CyrusOne to Bloomberg, via DatacenterDynamics). It occurred on the Thanksgiving-window reopen (evening of Nov 27, 2025, into Nov 28) as a hard freeze approached the Chicago suburbs. The confirmed mechanism is specifically the cooling-tower freeze-preparation/draining step being mishandled — which cascaded into a chiller-plant trip taking multiple cooling units offline. The fault sits in operating-procedure execution during a seasonal cold-weather changeover, not equipment age or a design defect. NOTE: the widely-repeated exact phrasing "preparing the cooling towers for freezing temperatures" is a paraphrase; the confirmed source wording describes staff/contractors failing to follow standard procedures when DRAINING cooling towers ahead of freezing weather.

LATENT / SYSTEMIC ROOT. First, MECHANICAL REDUNDANCY DID NOT CARRY THE LOAD: a single procedural lapse during freeze-prep took "multiple cooling units" down at once with no effective backup cooling path — a common-mode failure that a fault-tolerant plant with procedurally diverse changeover steps should have survived. CyrusOne's own remedy — it "installed additional redundancy to the cooling systems" (CyrusOne, confirmed verbatim via DCD) — is an admission that pre-incident backup cooling did not save the load. Second, CONCENTRATION RISK: CME ran globally-critical matching engines out of the single Aurora campus, so one plant's thermal failure halted worldwide futures/options price discovery. No chiller make/model, refrigerant, unit age, or the exact hydraulic detail (frozen tower basin, condenser-water freeze, free-cooling/glycol changeover valve, or low-ambient lockout) has been publicly disclosed — the confirmed record stops at the mishandled cooling-tower freeze-preparation.


## Contributing factors



- PROCEDURAL EXECUTION FAILURE DURING FREEZE-PREP (root, CONFIRMED): CyrusOne confirmed to Bloomberg that onsite staff and contractors failed to follow standard procedures when draining/preparing the cooling towers ahead of freezing weather (via DatacenterDynamics) - a seasonal cold-weather changeover mishandled on the live approach to a hard freeze.
- INADEQUATE / COMMON-MODE MECHANICAL REDUNDANCY: a single procedural lapse took 'multiple cooling units' offline at once with no backup cooling carrying the load, evidenced by CyrusOne's post-incident fix of having 'installed additional redundancy to the cooling systems' (confirmed verbatim via DCD) - i.e. the fault-tolerant protection a resilient plant should have provided was effectively absent for this failure mode.
- COLD-WEATHER / SEASONAL-TRANSITION TIMING RISK: the failure hit during a hard-freeze approach in the Chicago suburbs on the Thanksgiving-window reopen (evening of Nov 27, into Nov 28), a known high-risk winterization window for water-cooled tower plants, executed under live IT load (CyrusOne statement; DCD).
- SINGLE-SITE CONCENTRATION OF CRITICAL WORKLOAD: CME's matching engines ran from the single Aurora campus, so one plant's thermal failure halted global futures/options price discovery - a concentration-risk / missing geographic-diversity theme raised in trade commentary (attributed to DC Pulse; that specific commentary could not be independently re-fetched).
- CONTRACTOR-BOUNDARY / CHANGE-MANAGEMENT GAP: the lapse spanned both onsite personnel and contractors, implying a method-statement / supervision boundary where the freeze-prep steps were not verified - though no accessible source names the specific procedure document, the contracting firm, or which checklist step was skipped (disclosed uncertainty; CyrusOne via Bloomberg/DCD).



## Correction of errors (COE)



- Rebuild cooling-tower freeze-prep/winterization SOP as a checklist-gated changeover with independent two-person sign-off and seasonal dry-run CyrusOne Critical Facilities Operations · Not publicly confirmed (implied by stated root cause; only the redundancy fix was disclosed)
- Install additional redundancy to the CHI1 cooling systems CyrusOne · Done (CyrusOne confirmed it 'installed additional redundancy to the cooling systems')
- Restore stable and secure operations at CHI1 Aurora CyrusOne · Done (CyrusOne confirmed restored stable and secure operations)
- Impose change-management controls (method statements, supervision, two-person verify) at the contractor boundary for live freeze-prep CyrusOne / contracting firm · Not publicly confirmed
- Pursue geographically diverse cooling/power architecture for critical matching engines and review single-site concentration CME Group · Open / not publicly confirmed
- Wire thermal early-warning to automated IT load-shed thresholds (BMS/DCIM) CyrusOne / CME · Open / not publicly confirmed
- Regulatory awareness and market-integrity review of the outage CFTC / SEC · Reported aware/monitoring per Reuters (not independently reconfirmed)



## Lessons learnt



- A cooling plant is a single point of failure equal to any power system: a mishandled seasonal winterization step - not equipment age or a fire - halted a global exchange for ~11 hours, so freeze-prep is a critical, life-of-the-facility procedure, not routine maintenance.
- Redundancy that shares a common human/procedural mode is not redundancy: one mis-sequenced changeover took 'multiple cooling units' offline together, and the operator's after-the-fact addition of redundancy is proof the pre-incident backup path did not carry the load.
- Concentration risk is systemic risk: running globally-critical matching engines from one campus means one plant's thermal failure becomes worldwide market downtime - geographic diversity is a resilience requirement, not a luxury.
- Contractor-boundary work needs the tightest change control: because the lapse spanned staff and contractors, method statements, supervision, and independent verification must gate any live-load seasonal switchover.
- Detection must be wired to protection: rising hall temperatures should auto-trigger load-shed/throttling before safe inlet limits are crossed, rather than relying on a downstream tenant (CME) to halt compute to save the hardware.
- Public disclosure was partial: the operator confirmed human error and 'multiple cooling units' but never released chiller counts, refrigerant, peak sensor temperatures, or mobile-cooling tonnage - post-incidents should not be reconstructed as if those undisclosed specifics are established fact.



## Improvements & remediation



- Maintenance Rebuild the cooling-tower freeze-prep / winterization procedure as a verified, checklist-gated seasonal changeover with independent two-person sign-off - CyrusOne's own confirmed root cause is that staff and contractors failed to follow standard procedures when draining/preparing the cooling towers ahead of freezing weather, so procedure EXECUTION and verification, not just the document, must be hardened.
- Design Provide genuine common-mode-resistant mechanical redundancy (N+1/N+2 with procedurally diverse changeover steps) plus pre-staged rapid-response mobile cooling - implementing the very fix CyrusOne applied after the fact (it 'installed additional redundancy to the cooling systems').
- Process Institute change-management controls at the contractor boundary for any live freeze-prep switchover - approved method statements, on-site supervision, and a two-person verify step - since the lapse spanned both onsite personnel and contractors and no verification caught the mis-sequenced changeover before multiple units tripped.
- Safety Tighten thermal early-warning and automated load-shed thresholds (BMS/DCIM high-temp alarms tied to protective IT throttling) so a chiller-plant trip is caught and heat load shed before halls exceed safe inlet temperatures - closing detection-to-protection latency.
- Design/Resilience: For globally-critical workloads such as exchange matching engines, pursue redundant, geographically diverse cooling and power architectures so a single site's thermal failure cannot halt worldwide price discovery.
- Maintenance/Assurance: Run a pre-winter commissioning and dry-run of the full freeze-prep sequence each season, with an independent audit of tower drain-down, basin-heater energization, and free-cooling/glycol valve line-ups before the first hard freeze.



## Comprehensive analysis

### What happened

On the evening of Nov 27, 2025 (into Nov 28), CyrusOne's CHI1 (Chicago 1 / 'CH1') data center in Aurora, Illinois 'experienced a chiller plant failure affecting multiple cooling units' (CyrusOne, confirmed via DatacenterDynamics). Chilled-water cooling to the halls was lost as a hard freeze approached the Chicago suburbs, and CME Group - a tenant whose trading engines run from the campus - halted its markets to protect hardware. Trading resumed after roughly 11 hours. This was a loss-of-cooling (thermal) event, not a fire: there was no ignition, combustion, or suppression discharge.

### Why it happened (root and latent causes)

CyrusOne confirmed to Bloomberg the outage was caused by human error - onsite staff and contractors failed to follow standard procedures when draining/preparing the cooling towers ahead of freezing weather. Beneath that sit two latent gaps: (1) common-mode redundancy failure, since one mis-sequenced changeover took 'multiple cooling units' down together with no effective backup path - later confirmed by CyrusOne 'installing additional redundancy to the cooling systems'; and (2) single-site concentration of globally-critical workload. No chiller make/model, refrigerant, unit age, or exact hydraulic detail was disclosed.

### Why it mattered (impact and concentration risk)

Because CME's matching engines run from the single Aurora campus, a plant-level thermal failure became worldwide market downtime - traders lost access to futures prices for commodities and stocks across CME Group's derivatives markets for ~11 hours. Trade reporting listed benchmarks including S&P 500, Nasdaq, Treasuries, WTI, gold, Nikkei and palm oil (not independently reconfirmed here). The event also carried financial/reputational fallout: CyrusOne reportedly postponed a bond sale afterward (Bloomberg; not independently reconfirmed).

### Response and recovery

There was no suppression system to activate - the cooling plant itself was the failed 'suppression analogue.' Recovery was mechanical and manual: chillers were restarted at limited capacity and chilled-water circulation reconstituted until IT - and CME's markets - could be brought back in stages (EBS ~07:00 ET, full reopen ~08:30 ET per CNBC, not reconfirmed). CyrusOne then reported it 'restored stable and secure operations at its Chicago 1 (CHI1) data center' and 'installed additional redundancy to the cooling systems' (both confirmed verbatim).

### Verification status and source limitations

This review directly re-confirmed, via a reader-proxy to DatacenterDynamics relaying CyrusOne's statements: the CHI1/Aurora location, the 'chiller plant failure affecting multiple cooling units' phrasing, the human-error root cause tied to cooling-tower freeze-prep, the ~11-hour duration, the 109MW / 450,000 sq ft / 3-DC campus profile, and the two CyrusOne quotes on restored operations and added redundancy. It could NOT re-fetch Bloomberg, Reuters, CNBC or DC Pulse (bot-block/CAPTCHA) - so precise resume times, the CFTC/SEC line, the benchmark product list, the bond-sale detail, the $130M/15-year sale-leaseback, the >100degF temperature, and the 'temporary and supplemental chillers and pipework' phrase remain cited-but-not-independently-reconfirmed and, where noted, unverified.



## Technical deep-dive

 MECHANISM OF A COLD-WEATHER CHILLER-PLANT FAILURE. Paradoxically, this data-center thermal event was triggered by COLD, not heat. Water-cooled chiller plants reject heat through cooling towers that evaporate water to open air. When ambient temperatures approach and cross freezing, exposed condenser-water in tower basins, fill, and outdoor pipework can freeze, and the plant must be transitioned for cold weather — basins drained or heated, valves switched to free-cooling/glycol loops, flows and setpoints reconfigured — following a defined freeze-prep procedure. CyrusOne's confirmed account is that this changeover was executed incorrectly by onsite personnel and contractors who failed to follow standard procedures when preparing/draining the cooling towers ahead of freezing weather, and that this procedural lapse produced a chiller-plant failure affecting multiple cooling units (CyrusOne to Bloomberg, via DCD). The word "multiple" is the critical forensic signal: this was a COMMON-MODE trip, in which one mis-sequenced changeover simultaneously compromised more than one unit rather than a single random component failure that redundancy could absorb.

THERMAL CASCADE INTO IT. Data halls have low thermal mass relative to their heat load; against the campus's 109MW IT capacity, tens of megawatts of server heat with no chilled water raises room and rack-inlet temperatures within minutes. A widely-cited incident summary reports hall temperatures exceeding 100°F, but CyrusOne did NOT disclose a per-sensor peak — treat >100°F as an unverified reported figure, not a confirmed measurement. As inlet air crossed safe thresholds, the correct protective response is exactly what happened: shed the heat source. CME halted its trading systems — effectively an "evacuation of compute" — to stop generating heat and protect hardware while cooling was reconstituted, rather than risk mass server thermal damage.

RECONSTITUTION OF COOLING. There was no suppression system to activate because there was no fire; the "suppression analogue" — the cooling plant — was the very thing that failed. Recovery was mechanical and manual: chillers were restarted at limited capacity and cooling reconstituted until chilled-water circulation was stable enough to bring IT load — and CME's markets — back online in stages, with all trading resumed after roughly 11 hours. CyrusOne subsequently "installed additional redundancy to the cooling systems" and reported it "restored stable and secure operations" at CHI1 (both confirmed verbatim via DCD). NOTE ON UNCERTAINTY: no accessible primary source gives the exact minute the high-temperature threshold tripped, the peak hall temperature by sensor, the number of chillers affected versus total installed, or any mobile-chiller tonnage; the phrase "temporary and supplemental chillers and pipework" is attributed to a secondary trade blog (DC Pulse) that could not be re-fetched and does NOT appear in CyrusOne's DCD-relayed statement, so it is treated as unverified.

# Delta Air Lines Atlanta Data Center Power Failure Grounds the Global Fleet


 Delta Air Lines
 2016-08-08
 6h 0m core impact
 Power Fire


In the early hours of 8 August 2016, a routine scheduled transfer of load onto a backup generator at Delta Air Lines' Atlanta headquarters data center precipitated a fire in the power control room. The fire failed a transformer and cut a primary power path feeding the facility. Roughly 300 of Delta's 7,000 servers lacked a working alternate feed and went dark, and because surviving servers could no longer communicate with the failed nodes, the entire airline operations platform collapsed. Delta grounded its global fleet, cancelling about 2,100 flights over three days and delaying another 2,400, at an estimated cost of ~$150 million. CEO Ed Bastian took full responsibility. The event is a textbook case of a common-mode power fault upstream of server-level redundancy defeating an otherwise diverse design, compounded by a tightly-coupled system with no graceful degradation and an unmodernized legacy reservation tier.

## Root cause

 PROXIMATE IGNITION AND MECHANISM (verified core). A fire began at 2:30 AM EST on Monday, 8 August 2016 in the power-control room of Delta's data center at its Atlanta headquarters, and it was an electrical-equipment fire — "Delta, whose outage was caused by electrical-equipment failure" (Data Center Knowledge). Crucially, the ignition was triggered by a maintenance/test activity, not a random fault: "The fire was the result of a routine scheduled switch for testing purposes to the backup generator" (Availability Digest, verbatim). The verified physical mechanism is that the fire then destroyed a transformer: "The fire caused a transformer to fail, killing one of the two power feeds to the data center" (Availability Digest). Delta's and Georgia Power's public statements added component-level detail that this review could NOT independently re-verify this pass (source pages 403/404): Delta (COO Gil West / CEO Ed Bastian, as reported) called the failed item a "power control module" that "malfunctioned and caught fire, causing a surge to a Georgia Power transformer"; Georgia Power (spokesman John Kraft, as reported) called it "a switchgear... [that] malfunctioned for reasons that were not immediately clear," stressing "It was a failure of Delta equipment... there wasn't an area power outage." These are consistent with the verified spine but should be read as reported, not confirmed.\n\nCRITICAL DISCLOSURE GAP (well-supported). No manufacturer, model number, installation year, insulation type, or arc-fault-versus-mechanical-failure determination was ever publicly released. No official root-cause analysis, regulatory filing, or vendor status document exists; "for reasons that were not immediately clear" remained the effective ceiling on component-level causation. The physical failure mode is therefore officially unverified.\n\nLATENT ROOT — AS-BUILT REDUNDANCY DEFECT (verified). The catastrophe was not the fire, which was small and confined to the power-control room, but the redundancy defect it exposed. Delta's design intent was A+B power — "Each server in the data center has redundant power supplies, and each power supply is supposed to be plugged into different power strips" — but the as-built reality diverged: "300 of Delta's 7,000 servers in the data center were not linked to an alternate power source" (Availability Digest, verbatim). Those single-fed servers went down and "could not fail over to their backups, which were also down due to being unpowered." CEO Ed Bastian "took full responsibility for the failure" (Availability Digest); his widely-reported admission that the vulnerability "went undetected" is consistent but was not re-verified here.\n\nLATENT ROOT — TEST/TRANSFER AS TRIGGER + CONCENTRATED TRANSFER NODE. The true root cause is a stack: (1) a maintenance transfer sequence intended to prove resilience that instead ignited the gear ("result of a routine scheduled switch for testing purposes to the backup generator", verified); (2) an undetected A+B wiring defect on ~300 servers that no commissioning audit or failover test had caught (verified); and (3) a concentrated transfer/power node whose failure severed a utility feed and defeated failover simultaneously. The claim (analyst Robert Mann, EE Power, as reported — NOT re-verified) that "the switchgear failure locked Delta out of its reserve generators as well as from Georgia Power" describes this single-point-of-failure but rests on an unverified source; the verified facts alone (one feed killed + backups unpowered + whole system down) already establish that a single downstream event defeated a dual-utility-feed design.


## Contributing factors



- UNDETECTED AS-BUILT A+B WIRING DEFECT (commissioning/inspection lapse) — VERIFIED: design intent was every server's redundant PSUs on different power strips, but '300 of Delta's 7,000 servers... were not linked to an alternate power source' (Availability Digest). No commissioning audit or failover test had caught the design-vs-installation gap; CEO Bastian 'took full responsibility for the failure'.
- MAINTENANCE/TEST PROCEDURE AS THE TRIGGER — VERIFIED: the fire 'was the result of a routine scheduled switch for testing purposes to the backup generator' (Availability Digest). The resilience test itself ignited the gear, indicating the transfer sequence and/or the equipment's condition were inadequately de-risked before a live transfer.
- SINGLE DOWNSTREAM EVENT DEFEATED DUAL-FEED DESIGN — VERIFIED (mechanism) / REPORTED (nomenclature): a dual-utility-feed envelope was undone because one fire killed a transformer/feed AND left backups unpowered so failover failed. The specific 'switchgear failure locked Delta out of its reserve generators as well as from Georgia Power' framing (Robert Mann, EE Power) is as-reported and was not independently re-verified.
- TIGHT SYSTEM INTERDEPENDENCY / NO GRACEFUL DEGRADATION — VERIFIED: surviving servers 'could not communicate with the servers that failed. This took down Delta's entire system' (Availability Digest). Loss of only ~4% of servers collapsed the whole platform — insufficient partition tolerance / fault isolation.
- LEGACY-SYSTEM RECOVERY FRICTION — VERIFIED: the core reservation platform runs on 'a 52-year old legacy system called Deltamatic'; on restart 'only the old Deltamatic green-screen interface was operational', forcing manual check-in and handwritten boarding passes (Availability Digest) — extending impact far beyond power restoration.
- FAILURE-TO-FAIL-SAFE / SURGE PROPAGATION — REPORTED, NOT VERIFIED: Delta stated the failing module 'caus[ed] a surge to the transformer' (Gil West, ABC News, as reported), implying missing surge isolation/protective coordination. The verified record confirms only that 'the fire caused a transformer to fail', not the electrical surge mechanism.
- OPAQUE / ABSENT COMPONENT RCA — SUPPORTED BY ABSENCE: no make, model, age, or chemistry of the failed gear was ever disclosed and no official root-cause analysis, regulatory, or vendor document was published; Georgia Power could only say it failed 'for reasons that were not immediately clear' (as reported).
- UNDOCUMENTED FIRE-PROTECTION POSTURE — DISCLOSED GAP: no detection or fixed-suppression system is named in any verifiable source and no discharge is confirmed; the power-control room's fire-protection design and its performance were never validated in the public record.



## Correction of errors (COE)



- Public root-cause analysis identifying the failed component (make/model/age) and failure mechanism (arc-fault vs mechanical) Delta Air Lines (IT/Facilities) · Never published — official RCA absent (DISCLOSURE GAP)
- Correct the ~300 single-fed servers and audit dual-cord A/B integrity across all 7,000 servers Delta Air Lines (Data Center Operations) · Vulnerability acknowledged by CEO ('took full responsibility'); remediation completion not publicly verified
- Invest in IT resilience / modernize reservation and passenger-service platforms Delta Air Lines (CIO/CEO) · Delta publicly committed to IT-resilience investment post-incident; scope/completion not independently verified this pass
- Review switchgear/transfer maintenance and de-risk live generator-test transfer procedures Delta Air Lines (Facilities/Engineering) · Not publicly documented
- Confirm no area-grid cause and support Delta investigation Georgia Power · Georgia Power stated (as reported) it was Delta-equipment failure with 'no area power outage'; not re-verified this pass
- Validate power-control-room fire detection and fixed suppression design and performance Delta Air Lines (Facilities/Life-Safety) · No public evidence of any review — posture officially undocumented



## Lessons learnt



- Envelope redundancy is worthless without end-to-end integrity: two utility feeds 'through opposite sides of the building' did not help because a single fire killed a transformer/feed while ~300 servers' backups sat unpowered — redundancy must be verified continuously from utility entry to the individual server PSU, not assumed from design drawings.
- The resilience test can be the disaster: the ignition occurred during a scheduled transfer to the backup generator. Procedures meant to prove availability are high-energy events that must themselves be de-risked (condition-based maintenance, staged transfer, thermography) or they become the trigger.
- As-built drifts from design and only an audit catches it: 300 of 7,000 servers were mis-wired to a single feed and it 'went undetected' until a live fault. Dual-cord/failover integrity needs automated mapping and recurring drills, not one-time commissioning trust.
- Tight coupling turns a small fault into a total outage: losing ~4% of servers collapsed everything because survivors could not talk to the failed nodes. Systems need fault isolation and graceful degradation so partial infrastructure loss stays partial.
- Legacy monoliths dominate recovery time: a 52-year-old reservation system returning as green-screen-only forced handwritten boarding passes and stretched recovery across three days — technical debt is an availability risk, not just a modernization backlog item.
- Opacity undermines learning: with no published RCA and no disclosed make/model/age/chemistry, the true physical failure mode remains unverifiable years later; without forensic transparency the industry cannot prevent recurrence.
- Fire-protection design in electrical rooms must be explicit and tested: neither the detection nor the suppression system was ever documented publicly — undocumented protection is unvalidated protection.



## Improvements & remediation



- MAINTENANCE — De-risk live transfer/test procedures: since the fire 'was the result of a routine scheduled switch for testing purposes to the backup generator', treat generator/transfer testing as a high-energy operation: pre-test thermography and insulation-resistance checks on switchgear, breaker/relay maintenance records reviewed, and staged/loaded transfer under controlled conditions rather than a live full-load switch on aged gear.
- MAINTENANCE — Independent commissioning + periodic A/B integrity audits: the ~300 single-fed servers (out of 7,000) proves design intent diverged from as-built. Mandate dual-cord verification (physical trace of every PSU to independent, separately-fed PDUs/strips), automated per-outlet power-path mapping, and recurring pull-the-plug failover drills to catch wiring drift.
- SAFETY — Fire detection & fixed suppression validation in power-control rooms: the detection and suppression posture is officially undocumented. Install/verify aspirating (VESDA) very-early smoke detection and a fixed clean-agent (or pre-action) system in switchgear/power rooms, with documented discharge testing, arc-fault detection/mitigation, and coordinated auto de-energisation on fire alarm.
- SAFETY / ELECTRICAL — Protective coordination & surge isolation: introduce selective breaker coordination and surge/fault isolation so a faulting upstream device trips locally without propagating energy to and destroying a downstream transformer, eliminating the 'one fire kills a whole feed' failure mode.
- RESILIENCE — Remove concentrated single points of failure: audit the topology so no single switchgear, transfer switch, or transformer can simultaneously sever a utility feed and defeat generator failover; provide true 2N/isolated-bus separation with independent transfer paths.
- ARCHITECTURE — Graceful degradation / fault isolation: loss of ~4% of servers collapsed the entire platform because survivors 'could not communicate with the servers that failed'. Re-architect for partition tolerance, bulkheading, and degraded-mode operation so a partial power loss cannot take down the whole system.
- RECOVERY / IT — Modernize and geo-redundant the core platform: the 52-year-old Deltamatic monolith returning as green-screen-only forced manual check-in. Invest in a resilient, geographically-redundant reservation/DCS platform with tested automated failover to a second site.
- GOVERNANCE — Publish a real RCA and close the disclosure gap: no make/model/age/RCA of the failed gear was ever released. Adopt formal post-incident RCA with component forensics and maintenance-record review, feeding a tracked corrective-action register.



## Comprehensive analysis

### What is verified versus what remains reported-only

The verified spine (Availability Digest, read verbatim; corroborated on cause/cost by Data Center Knowledge) establishes: a fire at 2:30 AM EST on 8 Aug 2016 in the power-control room, triggered by a scheduled test-switch to the backup generator, destroyed a transformer and killed one of two feeds; ~300 of 7,000 servers were single-fed and their backups were unpowered; the whole system fell over; recovery took ~6 hours to 'operational' (8:30 AM), the ground stop lifted at 8:40 AM, and the airline cancelled 2,100 flights over three days at ~$150M. The component nomenclature — Delta's 'power control module' with a 'surge to the transformer', and Georgia Power's ' switchgear ... reasons not immediately clear' — comes from ABC News, the AJC, EE Power and NBC News that this review could not re-fetch this pass (HTTP 403/404, archive.org blocked, WebSearch budget exhausted). Those claims are retained as reported, not certified.

### The single-point-of-failure that defeated dual utility feeds

Delta built for backhoe protection — two utilities entering opposite sides of the building — yet a single overnight fire simultaneously killed a transformer/feed and left the ~300 single-fed servers' backups dead. Whether the precise 'switchgear locked Delta out of its reserve generators as well as from Georgia Power' framing (analyst Robert Mann, as reported) is exact or not, the verified facts already prove a concentrated downstream failure defeated an envelope-redundant design. The lesson is topological: redundancy must be verified as isolated and independent from utility entry all the way to each server's two power cords.

### Why a small, contained fire caused a global grounding

The fire never spread beyond the power-control room, yet it grounded the world's largest airline. Two amplifiers turned a ~4% power loss into a total outage: tight interdependency (survivors 'could not communicate with the servers that failed. This took down Delta's entire system') and legacy fragility (the 52-year-old Deltamatic core returned green-screen-only, forcing handwritten boarding passes). Extinguishing the fire did not restore service — the destroyed transformer, lost feed, and failed failover had already done the damage, and recovery was gated by manual reboots of ~500 servers and a brittle monolith.

### The official-RCA vacuum and source reliability

There is no official post-mortem : no Delta RCA, no regulatory or court filing, no vendor status page. The failed gear's make, model, age, insulation type, and failure mechanism were never disclosed; 'for reasons that were not immediately clear' is the effective ceiling. Fire detection and fixed suppression are entirely undocumented. Accordingly officialPostmortem is FALSE, approvedSources is limited to the two pages verified this pass (Availability Digest, Data Center Knowledge), and every component-level or emergency-response detail sourced to pages that returned 403/404 is flagged as reported-not-verified or struck.



## Technical deep-dive

 Delta's Atlanta data center was engineered for utility resilience at the building envelope: "Power is brought into Delta's data center from two separate utilities through opposite sides of the building to prevent power from being accidently cut with a back hoe" (Availability Digest, verbatim) — a classic backhoe-protection topology, with each server carrying redundant PSUs meant to draw from independent power strips. The 8 August event demonstrated that resilience at the envelope is worthless if a single downstream event can sever a source and defeat failover at the same time.\n\nVERIFIED FAILURE CHAIN (Availability Digest): (1) At 2:30 AM EST operators performed a scheduled transfer toward the backup generator for testing; the fire "was the result of" that switch. (2) A fire erupted in the power-control room. (3) "The fire caused a transformer to fail, killing one of the two power feeds to the data center." (4) Of ~7,000 servers, ~300 were wired only to the failed feed and lost power; "many of them could not fail over to their backups, which were also down due to being unpowered." (5) Even surviving servers "could not communicate with the servers that failed. This took down Delta's entire system" — a small (~4%) power loss collapsed the whole platform through tight interdependency.\n\nREPORTED-BUT-UNVERIFIED COMPONENT DETAIL: Delta publicly attributed the event to a "power control module" that "malfunctioned, causing a surge to the transformer and a loss of power" (Gil West, ABC News, as reported); Georgia Power attributed it to "a switchgear... malfunctioned for reasons that were not immediately clear" and insisted it was "a failure of Delta equipment... there wasn't an area power outage" (John Kraft, as reported). This review could not re-fetch those pages (HTTP 403/404) and does not treat the "surge" mechanism or the "switchgear/module" nomenclature as confirmed — the verified account is only that a fire, triggered by a test transfer, destroyed a transformer and killed one feed.\n\nRECOVERY: Manual recovery was severe — "500 servers had to be rebooted. It wasn't until 8:30 AM, six hours later, that the Delta systems were once again operational." When Delta's core platform returned it did so degraded: the reservation/passenger-service systems run on "a 52-year old legacy system called Deltamatic," and "only the old Deltamatic green-screen interface was operational," forcing agents to "manually check[] in passengers and handwrit[e] boarding passes" (Availability Digest, verbatim). The FAA ground stop lifted at 8:40 AM, but by 1:30 PM "only 1,700 of Delta's scheduled 6,000 flights were in operation," and operational recovery stretched three days (2,100 cancellations; 2,400 delays; ~$150M cost).\n\nFORENSIC UNKNOWNS (disclosed). No public source names the fire-DETECTION system (aspirating/VESDA, spot smoke, or heat) or the detection moment — the only fixed data point is the 2:30 AM origin. No source documents any fixed SUPPRESSION system (clean-agent gaseous, pre-action sprinkler, or none) or confirms a discharge; extinguishment characterizations ("a small fire that was quickly extinguished"; "firefighters were called") appear only in secondary trade/retrospective material this review could not re-fetch and does not certify. No evacuation and no injuries were reported, consistent with an unmanned overnight electrical-room fire. Critically, extinguishing the fire did not restore service — the destroyed transformer, the lost feed, and the failed failover had already done the damage.

## Sequence of events (SOE)




- 2023-05-21T01:40 (local PT) TRIGGER Fire breaks out in a specific equipment rack in the Colo 4 colocation suite at Digital Realty LAX12, 2260 E El Segundo Blvd, El Segundo; ignition cause undetermined. Time per an Evocative incident report cited by DCD.
- 2023-05-21T01:40 (local PT, approx) DETECTION No aspirating/VESDA smoke detection or first-alarm time is documented in any source; the earliest recorded protection response is the heat-activated sprinkler, implying heat/smoke had already built up in the cabinet before any alarm on record.
- 2023-05-21 (early AM) MITIGATION The fire sprinkler system activates in the Colo space above row 4 (water suppression; sub-type not disclosed by sources), discharging onto the IT load below.
- 2023-05-21 (early AM) MITIGATION Sprinkler discharge contains the fire — 'limited to row 4 with some exposure to adjacent rows' per a Digital Realty report cited by DCD — effective as a fire-stop.
- 2023-05-21 (early AM) CASCADE Sprinkler water inflicts collateral damage: the discharge 'result[ed] in water damage to many servers' in the colocation space, shifting the loss mode from thermal to hydraulic.
- 2023-05-21 (early AM) MITIGATION Fire department responds and closes two colocation suites (Colo 3 and Colo 4) — 'Two colo halls closed by fire department after a blaze in the racks.' No call/arrival time, apparatus count, or on-scene tactics are public.
- 2023-05-21 (early AM) MITIGATION 'Power was cut off to the Colo 3 and 4 spaces' as part of the fire-response de-energisation.
- 2023-05-21 (early AM) CASCADE De-energisation reaches the unburned Colo 3 suite — a tenant reported it 'appears to be safe' — taking down customers whose racks were never on fire; cross-suite impact beyond the fire origin (physical adjacency inferred, not stated).
- 2023-05-21 (~1 hour after shutdown) RECOVERY 'Power was restored to Colo 3 after an hour or so'; the unburned suite comes back while Colo 4 remains de-energised.
- 2023-05-21 (early AM) IMPACT No fire spread beyond the two suites; event contained to Colo 4 row 4 plus limited adjacent-row exposure. No injury statement appears in any source (record is silent, not an affirmative zero).
- 2023-05-22 (Monday) IMPACT Aftermath: a Colo 3 tenant reports the lobby 'absolutely packed with people waiting to get access to Colo 4,' conference rooms that 'looked like a battle zone,' and 'The smell of smoke was intense, and the cleaning chemicals too.' Some users still locked out a day later.
- 2023-05-22 to 2023-05-24 IMPACT Evocative (operating as Krypt, holding former VPLS/INAP assets) loses an unknown number of servers; water damage was 'particularly severe' for it.
- 2023-05-24 (Wednesday, late) IMPACT Colo 4 still without power roughly three days after the fire; a tenant reports 'I contacted Digital Reality and they were tight-lipped, only responding with empty words' — no recovery ETA communicated.
- 2023-05 (several days after) RECOVERY Colo 4 'remained out of commission for several days' before restoration; recovery bounded by water-damage remediation and equipment replacement rather than fire repair.
- 2023-05-25 (Thursday) RESTORED DataCenterDynamics (Peter Judge) publishes the only primary press account and states it has contacted Digital Realty for more information; cause remains officially 'undetermined' and no operator or fire-authority root-cause analysis is subsequently published.



## Root cause

 PROXIMATE IGNITION — OFFICIALLY UNDETERMINED. The only cause statement in the public record is negative: "Despite ongoing investigations, the exact cause of the fire remains undetermined" (Dgtl Infra). What is established is the location and load class of ignition, not the mechanism. The fire began at 1:40am on Sunday 21 May 2023 in the Colo 4 colocation suite at Digital Realty's LAX12 facility, 2260 E El Segundo Blvd — it "originated in a specific rack" (Dgtl Infra), on the raised-floor IT/colo load inside a customer cabinet in (or under the sprinkler zone above) row 4, NOT in a discrete UPS room, battery room, or generator plant. No public source names the make, model, age, or battery/cell chemistry of the originating equipment, and it is not confirmed whether the first item to ignite was a server power supply, a PDU or rack whip, a cable bundle, or an in-rack battery. The facility carried 7.45 MW of UPS capacity across a two-story 132,000 sq ft building (Dgtl Infra), but no source connects that UPS/battery plant to the ignition — this is a colocation-rack IT-load fire, not a documented energy-storage event.

LATENT ROOT — WATER-BASED SUPPRESSION IN A LIVE COLO HALL. The forensically significant latent factor is the fire-protection design of the colo hall: it was protected by a water sprinkler that discharged onto energised IT. The sprinkler type is NOT disclosed by any source (only "fire sprinkler system"/"sprinkler system"), so a wet-pipe vs pre-action determination cannot be made from the record — but water DID reach the racks, which drove the damage profile. As a fire-STOP the sprinkler worked: activation "above row 4... was limited to row 4 with some exposure to adjacent rows" (Digital Realty via DCD). But water is indiscriminate: the same discharge "result[ed] in water damage to many servers" (Dgtl Infra) and contributed to an "unknown number of servers" destroyed (DCD). Whether early aspirating detection plus clean-agent suppression was present is not evidenced either way — neither is named in any source — so the mitigation gap is a documented absence of evidence, not a confirmed design defect.

LATENT ROOT — CROSS-SUITE DE-ENERGISATION COUPLING. Power was cut to both Colo 3 and Colo 4 when the fire department closed the halls (DCD). Colo 3, which a tenant reported "appears to be safe," still lost power (restored "after an hour or so"); Colo 4 stayed dark for several days. That the fire-response envelope forced de-energisation of a second, unburned suite points to electrical/zoning and life-safety-shutdown coupling between neighbouring colo spaces — a factor that widened the customer-impact blast radius beyond the room that actually burned. (Physical adjacency of the two suites is inferred, not stated.)

MAINTENANCE / INSPECTION ROOT — NOT DETERMINABLE FROM THE RECORD. No public source implicates or exonerates any maintenance, inspection, or testing lapse. There is no hot-work or energised-work record, no deferred-inspection finding, and no sprinkler or detection test history in evidence. Because Digital Realty published no root-cause analysis and was described by a tenant as "tight-lipped," a maintenance chain can neither be confirmed nor excluded. The honest root-cause statement is therefore two-part: proximate ignition genuinely undetermined; latent contribution traceable to water-based suppression discharging on live IT and to cross-suite power-shutdown coupling.


## Contributing factors



- Fire-protection design: the colo hall was protected by a water sprinkler that discharged onto live IT — activation contained the fire but 'result[ed] in water damage to many servers' (Dgtl Infra), converting a single-rack fire into a wet loss across the row and adjacent rows (sprinkler sub-type not disclosed by sources).
- Detection design not evidenced: no smoke/VESDA aspirating detection system and no first-alarm time appear in any public source — the only mitigation element on record is the heat-activated sprinkler, which by nature acts only after significant heat has built up, and any earlier incipient-stage response is undocumented (forensic).
- Cross-suite power coupling: de-energisation forced by the fire response cut power to a second suite (Colo 3) as well as the fire-origin Colo 4 — 'Power was cut off to the Colo 3 and 4 spaces' (DCD) — widening customer impact beyond the room that burned; Colo 3 was reported 'safe' yet still lost power for about an hour.
- Undetermined ignition on the colo IT load: the fire 'originated in a specific rack' (Dgtl Infra) with no confirmed device, chemistry, or failure mode — the officially 'undetermined' cause (Dgtl Infra) means no corrective action could target the true initiating fault.
- Operator transparency/communication gap: a tenant reported Digital Realty was 'tight-lipped, only responding with empty words' (Reddit via DCD) and the operator issued no substantive public statement or published root-cause analysis, leaving affected customers without recovery ETAs during a multi-day Colo 4 outage.
- Maintenance/inspection history not evidenced either way: no sprinkler/detection test records, hot-work permits, or deferred-inspection findings are in the public record, so a maintenance lapse can neither be confirmed nor excluded (forensic) — an evidentiary gap that itself impedes prevention.



## Correction of errors (COE)



- Obtain the El Segundo/LA County Fire Department incident report and the Evocative and Digital Realty internal reports to establish the confirmed ignition source and suppression sub-type Facility operator / fire authority · Not evidenced as done (cause remains officially undetermined)
- Assess colo-hall detection/suppression: add VESDA + clean-agent or convert to double-interlock pre-action to prevent water on live IT Data-center engineering · No public evidence of remediation
- Re-zone life-safety power shutdown so an unburned neighbouring suite is not de-energised with the fire-origin suite Electrical / MEP design · No public evidence of remediation
- Publish a customer incident-communication SLA with status-page updates and recovery ETAs Operator customer-success / comms · No public evidence of remediation
- Commission and disclose an independent root-cause analysis for the fire Digital Realty · Not published as of the sources



## Lessons learnt



- Water as a colo suppressant is a double-edged control: the sprinkler stopped fire spread yet 'result[ed] in water damage to many servers' (Dgtl Infra) — containment success and asset destruction came from the same discharge, so suppression choice materially shapes the loss.
- Blast radius is set by shutdown zoning, not just by flame: an unburned suite (Colo 3) still went dark because 'Power was cut off to the Colo 3 and 4 spaces' (DCD) — electrical/life-safety coupling between suites can multiply customer impact.
- Heat-activated suppression is inherently late: with no VESDA/first-alarm evidenced, the first recorded response was a sprinkler that only trips after significant heat, foreclosing any incipient-stage de-energisation before flame (forensic).
- Silence is an incident cost: a tenant's 'tight-lipped, only responding with empty words' (Reddit via DCD) shows that absent ETAs and status updates amplify business disruption independent of the physical damage.
- An 'undetermined' cause with no published RCA is a prevention gap in itself: without a named initiating fault (Dgtl Infra), neither operator nor industry can close the loop on the true failure mode.
- Concentration risk is real for managed tenants: Evocative/Krypt (former VPLS/INAP assets) took 'particularly severe' damage (Dgtl Infra), a reminder that a single suite event can disproportionately hit one customer's estate.



## Improvements & remediation



- Safety Add a two-stage strategy to live colo halls — very-early aspirating smoke detection (VESDA) cross-zoned to a gaseous clean-agent suppression system — so an incipient rack fire is knocked down before flashover without soaking energised IT, the exact collateral that here 'result[ed] in water damage to many servers' (Dgtl Infra). Where water sprinklers remain code-required, use double-interlock pre-action so no water sits over the racks until both heat and smoke confirm.
- Maintenance Institute and retain a documented test/inspection regime for detection and suppression — periodic sprinkler flow/trip tests, VESDA sensitivity checks, and rack-level thermal/arc-fault inspections — since the public record contains no maintenance history and a lapse could be neither confirmed nor excluded (forensic).
- Design Decouple life-safety power shutdown between colo suites so a fire-response de-energisation of the origin suite (Colo 4) does not force an outage on a neighbour reported 'safe' (Colo 3 lost ~1 hour of power for a fire it did not have) (DCD).
- Process Establish a customer incident-communication protocol with committed status-page updates and recovery ETAs; a tenant described the operator as 'tight-lipped, only responding with empty words' (Reddit via DCD) through a multi-day Colo 4 outage, compounding business impact.
- Safety Deploy in-cabinet fire detection/early suppression and rack-level current/arc monitoring so a single-cabinet ignition is isolated at the rack rather than fought at the room ceiling after heat build-up.
- Process Commission and disclose an independent root-cause investigation for undetermined-cause IT fires; leaving the cause 'undetermined' (Dgtl Infra) with no published RCA prevents the operator and the wider industry from targeting the true initiating fault.



## Comprehensive analysis

### What burned, and what did not

This was a colocation IT-load fire, not a plant event. The fire 'originated in a specific rack' (Dgtl Infra) in Colo 4 at LAX12 (2260 E El Segundo Blvd) at 1:40am on 21 May 2023. Despite the facility's 7.45 MW UPS plant across 132,000 sq ft, no source links UPS or batteries to ignition — the origin was a customer cabinet on the raised floor, and the cause remains officially 'undetermined' (Dgtl Infra).

### Suppression: a fire-stop that became a water loss

The sprinkler 'was activated in the Colo space above row 4 and was limited to row 4 with some exposure to adjacent rows' (Digital Realty via DCD) — an effective fire-stop. But it 'result[ed] in water damage to many servers' (Dgtl Infra), turning a thermal event into a hydraulic one. The sprinkler sub-type (wet-pipe vs pre-action) is not disclosed by any source, and no VESDA or clean-agent system is named — an absence of evidence, not a confirmed design defect.

### Cross-suite de-energisation widened the impact

The fire department closed two suites and 'Power was cut off to the Colo 3 and 4 spaces' (DCD). Colo 3, which a tenant said 'appears to be safe,' still lost power (restored 'after an hour or so'), while Colo 4 'remained out of commission for several days' (Dgtl Infra) and was still dark ~3 days later (DCD). The shutdown envelope, not the flame, set the customer blast radius .

### Communication and evidentiary gaps

A tenant found the operator 'tight-lipped, only responding with empty words' (Reddit via DCD); no operator statement or root-cause analysis was published. The fire-authority incident report, injury status, dollar loss, server count, water-flow figures, and emergency-response chronometry are all absent from the record. The forensic picture is firm on sequence and suppression class and empty on ignition mechanism — gaps that are disclosed, not filled by inference.



## Technical deep-dive

 This was an IT-load rack fire on a raised-floor colocation hall, not a plant-room (UPS/battery/generator) event, and the physical story turns on the water sprinkler. At 1:40am on 21 May 2023 a specific cabinet in Colo 4 at LAX12 ignited from an undetermined cause. "The fire sprinkler system was activated in the Colo space above row 4 and was limited to row 4 with some exposure to adjacent rows, according to a report from Digital Realty" (via DCD). Sprinkler heads are heat-activated at the head, so visible/energetic combustion and hot smoke had already developed in the cabinet before any water flowed. The sprinkler TYPE is not disclosed in any source — the record does not establish wet-pipe versus pre-action, and any specific head-rating or fusible-link temperature would be inference, not evidence. Likewise, no aspirating/VESDA smoke detection and no gaseous clean-agent suppression is NAMED anywhere in the record; that is an absence of evidence, not a confirmed absence of the systems.

Once discharging, the sprinkler put water onto energised IT below. This is the crux of the damage mechanics: suppression stopped fire propagation but soaked the row — the discharge "result[ed] in water damage to many servers" (Dgtl Infra) — so the loss mode shifted from thermal to hydraulic. The fire department closed two colocation suites (Colo 3 and Colo 4) and "Power was cut off to the Colo 3 and 4 spaces" (DCD). Colo 3, reported by a tenant as "safe," was re-energised "after an hour or so"; Colo 4, the fire origin, "remained out of commission for several days" (Dgtl Infra) and was still without power when a tenant posted "late on Wednesday," roughly three days after the fire (DCD). Evocative — operating as Krypt and holding former VPLS/INAP assets — "lost an unknown number of servers" (DCD), with water damage "particularly severe" for it (Dgtl Infra).

What the physical record does NOT contain is as important as what it does: no first-alarm time, no fire-department call/dispatch/arrival timestamps, no apparatus count, no on-scene tactics or incident-command detail, no water-flow or discharge-duration figure, no temperature reading, no confirmed server count, no dollar loss, no injury statement, and no confirmed ignition device. The El Segundo/LA County fire incident report could not be located, and the Reddit thread and any Evocative status-page report were not directly accessible. The forensic picture is firm on sequence and suppression class (a water sprinkler, activated, effective as a fire-stop, damaging as a collateral hazard) and empty on ignition mechanism, suppression sub-type, and emergency-services chronometry.

Li-ion UPS fire forced emergency power shutdown, impacting customers incl. Alibaba/Lazada — sub-scores ESTIMATED from public impact reporting, pending deep research.



## Sequence of events (SOE)




- 2024-09-10 morning SGT TRIGGER Electrical fault in a third-floor mezzanine battery room initiates Li-ion thermal runaway at the Digital Realty Digital Loyang data center, Loyang, Singapore. 'Early investigations suggest an electrical issue in one of the battery rooms triggered the blaze.'
- 2024-09-10 morning SGT DETECTION Building fire-alarm system activates — the first publicly indicated detection event; no discrete smoke/heat-sensor timing is disclosed beyond this alarm.
- 2024-09-10 morning SGT MITIGATION Facility sprinkler systems activate over the involved battery/power rooms on the third-floor mezzanine.
- 2024-09-10 before arrival MITIGATION About 20 occupants self-evacuate the building before firefighters arrive.
- 2024-09-10 morning SGT MITIGATION SCDF alerted and responds to the Loyang data centre to secure the premises and stabilise the situation.
- 2024-09-10 ~08:15 SGT MITIGATION All on-site personnel evacuated with no injuries; SCDF deploys four water jets to cool and contain the battery fire.
- 2024-09-10 daytime IMPACT Alibaba Cloud detects network anomalies in Singapore Availability Zone C; Lazada and ByteDance/TikTok begin experiencing service disruption.
- 2024-09-10 daytime CASCADE Alibaba warns of increasing likelihood of a complete network outage in Availability Zone C if battery-room temperatures are not controlled; O&M engineers are unable to enter the building.
- 2024-09-10 evening SGT MITIGATION SCDF firefighting knocks down / contains the blaze after roughly half a day of cooling; operation flagged as prolonged due to battery cooling requirements (exact containment time per DCD reconstruction, not re-verified this pass).
- 2024-09-10 overnight to 2024-09-11 IMPACT Firefighting and sprinkler water accumulates and leaks into server halls; Alibaba reports 'water accumulation and leaks, posing a risk of electrical short circuits.'
- 2024-09-11 early hours SGT CASCADE Emergency power shutdown of the affected building executed to prevent electrical short circuits from standing water — this de-energisation, not flame, takes Alibaba Cloud Availability Zone C fully offline (~01:46 per DCD, not re-verified this pass).
- 2024-09-11 second day MITIGATION Operation spills into a second day; an unmanned firefighting robot is deployed for damping-down as manual entry remains too hazardous/hot.
- 2024-09-12 RECOVERY SCDF declares the site stable after multi-day cooling and damping-down operations.
- post-fire (Sep 2024) RECOVERY BCA assesses the structure: minor plaster delamination, paint peeling and soot only, structural integrity intact; issues closure orders for portions of the third, fourth floors and mezzanine.
- post-stabilisation (Sep 2024) RESTORED Alibaba carefully dries water-exposed hardware to ensure data security; migration and restoration of affected machinery proceeds as planned.



## Root cause

 Ignition source: the facility's lithium-ion battery bank serving the UPS/energy-storage backup of Digital Realty's Digital Loyang data center in Loyang, Singapore, housed in battery rooms on the third-floor mezzanine of the four-storey building. Press relaying SCDF reported the fire "involved lithium-ion batteries housed in battery rooms on the third floor." Proximate mechanism: thermal runaway initiated by an electrical fault — "Early investigations suggest an electrical issue in one of the battery rooms triggered the blaze" (Straits Times/SCDF). Once initiated, cell-to-cell thermal-runaway propagation — the self-sustaining, re-igniting behaviour characteristic of Li-ion cells — resisted extinguishment and forced prolonged cooling that spilled into a second day.

DISCLOSED UNCERTAINTY: The public record does not disclose the battery/UPS make and model, the cell chemistry (NMC vs LFP), cell age, state of charge, or the precise electrical fault (internal cell short vs charger/BMS fault vs connection arc). No make/model/chemistry can be attributed without over-claiming. The specific Digital Realty site code and exact street address are not independently confirmed in this review pass and are therefore not asserted.

LATENT ROOT — DESIGN/SITING, NOT A MAINTENANCE VIOLATION: The salient systemic root is battery-room placement. SCDF's 2020 safety standards require Energy Storage Systems (Li-ion battery rooms) to sit on the ground floor, but the failed batteries were on the third-floor mezzanine. Digital Realty's position is that the facility launched in 2016, before the 2020 standard, so the elevated placement predated and was not governed by that rule — a legacy/grandfathered design rather than a rules breach (DCD). This above-grade siting materially worsened the event: it complicated firefighter access and battery cooling, and it placed burning batteries within the same structure as live server halls, so suppression water drained down into the IT space and forced an emergency power shutdown. No public evidence identifies a maintenance, inspection, testing, hot-work, or deferred-work lapse as the ignition cause; the trigger is described only as "an electrical issue in one of the battery rooms." The dominant redundancy/design gap is therefore the co-location of an above-grade Li-ion energy-storage hazard above critical IT load, with water-based suppression as the only viable firefighting medium.


## Contributing factors



- Legacy above-grade battery siting: Li-ion energy-storage rooms were on the third-floor mezzanine, contrary to SCDF's 2020 standard requiring ground-floor placement. Digital Realty states the 2016 facility predated the rule, so it was grandfathered — but the elevated siting is the single largest aggravating design factor (DCD).
- Water-based suppression against Li-ion thermal runaway: sprinklers plus four SCDF water jets could only cool, not stop, self-sustaining cell-to-cell propagation, forcing a multi-day operation and generating the water volume that later reached the IT halls (Straits Times/SCDF).
- Vertical co-location of burning batteries above live server halls: with no water-tight separation between the third-floor battery rooms and IT space, suppression water accumulated and leaked into server rooms, creating the short-circuit risk that drove the emergency shutdown (DCD; Alibaba via DCD).
- Firefighting-protocol lockout of operators: Alibaba's operation-and-maintenance engineers were unable to enter the building, delaying damage assessment, drying and restoration of water-exposed hardware (DCD).
- Single-facility concentration risk for tenants: Alibaba Cloud Singapore Availability Zone C, and downstream Lazada and ByteDance/TikTok, had insufficient isolation from a single building event, so one battery-room fire produced a multi-tenant regional outage (DCD; The Star).
- No public evidence of a maintenance/inspection/testing lapse: the trigger is described only as 'an electrical issue in one of the battery rooms,' with battery make/model, chemistry, age and state of charge undisclosed — an evidentiary gap rather than a confirmed clean bill (Straits Times/SCDF).



## Correction of errors (COE)



- Relocate/segregate Li-ion ESS battery rooms to ground-floor, water-contained enclosures per SCDF 2020 ESS standard Digital Realty (facility engineering) · Open — no public completion evidence
- Install water-tight bunding/drainage between battery rooms and server halls to prevent suppression-water ingress into IT space Digital Realty (design/build) · Open — no public evidence
- Deploy thermal-runaway-appropriate detection and suppression (cell-level/gas/aerosol) to shorten cooling and cut water volume Digital Realty with SCDF guidance · Open — no public evidence
- Dry, assess and restore water-exposed hardware to ensure data security Alibaba Cloud O&M · In progress — migration and restoration reported proceeding as planned (DCD)
- Building-integrity assessment and closure orders for affected floors BCA / SCDF · Completed — structural integrity intact; closure orders issued (BCA/Straits Times)
- Root-cause investigation of the battery-room electrical fault (make/model/chemistry/age) SCDF / Digital Realty · Early investigation only — findings not publicly disclosed (Straits Times)



## Lessons learnt



- Against Li-ion thermal runaway, water suppresses nothing — it only cools; sprinklers and four water jets could not stop cell-to-cell propagation, turning the event into a multi-day cooling operation (Straits Times/SCDF).
- The suppressant became the primary weapon of collateral damage: firefighting/sprinkler water, not flame, reached the server halls and forced the emergency power shutdown that caused the actual outage (DCD; Alibaba via DCD).
- Vertical siting of an ESS hazard above IT load converts a contained battery fire into a facility-wide IT event through simple gravity-driven water migration (DCD).
- Grandfathered/legacy compliance is not the same as safe design: the 2016 above-grade battery rooms were legal because they predated the 2020 ground-floor standard, yet that very placement drove the worst consequences (DCD).
- Operator lockout under fire-safety protocol lengthens recovery — barring O&M engineers from the building delayed drying and restoration of water-exposed hardware (DCD).
- Single-building faults still cascade to whole cloud Availability Zones; tenant redundancy that shares one physical facility is insufficient isolation (DCD; The Star).



## Improvements & remediation



- Design Relocate Li-ion energy-storage systems to ground-floor, water-segregated rooms per SCDF's 2020 ESS standard so burning batteries are not sited above live server halls and suppression water cannot drain into IT space (basis: DCD siting finding).
- Design Introduce water-tight bunding, drainage and floor-slab containment between battery rooms and IT halls so sprinkler/firefighting water from an ESS event is captured and drained rather than pooling on energised equipment (basis: Alibaba water-ingress report via DCD).
- Safety Supplement or replace water-only suppression in Li-ion battery rooms with thermal-runaway-appropriate measures (cell-level detection, gas/aerosol early suppression, dedicated cooling) to shorten the multi-day cooling operation and reduce suppression-water volume (basis: SCDF 'prolonged' cooling requirement, Straits Times).
- Process Establish a pre-agreed operator re-entry and safe-shutdown protocol with SCDF so O&M engineers can perform controlled de-energisation and hardware protection earlier, rather than being unable to enter the building during the critical window (basis: DCD).
- Maintenance Institute and document battery-room electrical-integrity monitoring (BMS fault logging, connection/thermal inspection, state-of-charge and cell-age tracking) to close the evidentiary gap around 'an electrical issue' and enable pre-failure detection (basis: undisclosed cause / no public inspection record, Straits Times).
- Design Improve tenant availability-zone isolation so a single-building event cannot take an entire cloud Availability Zone (and downstream Lazada/TikTok) offline via one power shutdown (basis: multi-tenant cascade, DCD/The Star).



## Comprehensive analysis

### A thermal-runaway fire, but a water-caused outage

The September 2024 fire at Digital Realty's Digital Loyang facility is best understood as two coupled events. The first was a lithium-ion battery fire on the third-floor mezzanine, triggered by an electrical fault and sustained by cell-to-cell thermal runaway that water can cool but not extinguish. The second — and the one that actually caused the customer-visible outage — was hydraulic: accumulated sprinkler and firefighting water draining down into server halls, forcing an emergency power shutdown to avoid short circuits. Flame never breached the IT space or structural integrity; the suppressant did the damage.

### Above-grade battery siting as the systemic root

The decisive design condition was that an energy-storage hazard sat above live server halls with no water-tight separation. SCDF's 2020 ESS standard requires Li-ion battery rooms on the ground floor precisely to avoid this geometry; the failed rooms were on the third-floor mezzanine. Gravity did the rest — water migrated down onto energised equipment. Ground-floor siting with bunded, drained containment would have decoupled the battery event from the IT load.

### Legacy compliance versus safe design

Digital Realty's stated position is that the facility launched in 2016, before the 2020 standard, so the elevated placement was grandfathered rather than a breach. That is legally coherent but operationally cautionary: the arrangement that was permissible under the older code is exactly the arrangement that turned a contained battery fire into a regional cloud outage. Grandfathered compliance is not evidence of safe design.

### The multi-tenant cascade

Because a single building hosted Alibaba Cloud Singapore Availability Zone C, the emergency de-energisation propagated outward — first to Alibaba's own AZ-C, then to downstream tenants Lazada and ByteDance/TikTok. The blast radius demonstrates that logical availability-zone labels do not guarantee physical isolation when redundancy is concentrated in one structure. Recovery was further slowed by fire-safety protocol barring O&M engineers from re-entry until the site was declared stable.

### Evidentiary gaps that remain open

The public record does not disclose the battery/UPS make and model, cell chemistry, age, state of charge, or the precise electrical fault. The trigger is described only as 'an electrical issue in one of the battery rooms.' No maintenance, inspection or hot-work lapse is identified — which is an absence of evidence, not a clean bill. A full root cause would require the undisclosed SCDF/Digital Realty investigation findings, which were not public as of this review.



## Technical deep-dive

 The event is a textbook illustration of why Li-ion energy storage co-located with IT load creates a cascading, water-coupled failure mode rather than a contained electrical fire. On the morning of 10 Sep 2024 the building fire-alarm system triggered — the first publicly indicated detection event; no discrete smoke/heat-sensor timing is disclosed beyond the alarm. Facility sprinklers activated and SCDF deployed four water jets on arrival. Crucially, water is a coolant, not an extinguishant, for Li-ion thermal runaway: it cannot arrest cell-to-cell propagation, only remove heat, so the fire re-asserted itself and the operation became a prolonged cooling exercise — contained the same day but requiring damping-down with an unmanned firefighting robot (conditions too hot/hazardous for manual entry) and not declared stable until 12 Sep.

The decisive engineering failure was hydraulic, not thermal. Because the battery rooms sat on the third-floor mezzanine directly within the four-storey structure, accumulated firefighting and sprinkler water migrated downward into server halls. Alibaba reported the server room "started to experience water accumulation and leaks, posing a risk of electrical short circuits." To prevent energised electronics from short-circuiting in standing water, an emergency power shutdown of the affected building was executed in the early hours of 11 Sep — roughly 18 hours after the alarm per DCD's reconstruction of Alibaba's timeline. This de-energisation, not flame, is what took Alibaba Cloud Singapore Availability Zone C fully offline and cascaded to Lazada and ByteDance/TikTok. The fire itself never breached structural integrity: BCA found only minor plaster delamination, paint peeling and soot, and issued closure orders for portions of the third, fourth and mezzanine levels. Recovery was throttled by fire-safety protocol — Alibaba's O&M engineers were barred from re-entering the building — so wet hardware had to be carefully dried before migration/restoration. The lesson embedded in the physics: with an above-grade Li-ion hazard and water-only suppression, the suppressant becomes the primary agent of collateral IT damage.

# Dyn Managed DNS Outage — Mirai IoT Botnet DDoS (October 21, 2016)


 Dyn
 2016-10-21
 11h 0m core impact
 Network Software


On Friday 21 October 2016, Dyn's managed (authoritative) DNS platform was hit by a large-scale distributed denial-of-service attack in which a Mirai-malware IoT botnet directed a flood of DNS lookup requests at the service. The attack arrived in three windows across the day (UTC 11:10-13:20, 15:50-17:00, 20:00-22:10). Because so many major properties delegated their NS records to Dyn, the attack cascaded into user-visible outages for several dozen named services — including Twitter, Reddit, Spotify, Netflix, GitHub and PayPal — across the United States and Europe for much of the day. Dyn reported receiving malicious requests from tens of millions of IP addresses; the compromised endpoints were consumer devices such as printers, IP cameras, residential gateways and baby monitors, not spoofed traffic.
