 | Emergency-services / fire-brigade calls and arrivals | 0 - none reported |
 | Lingering storage damage (Google) | Small percentage of replicated Persistent Disks in single-redundant mode; small number of HDD-backed PD volumes exhibiting IO errors |
 | Operators impacted by the same heat event (same day) | 2 - Google (europe-west2-a) and Oracle (UK South) |




## Magnitude profile


 Magnitude **5.2** = blast 6×0.35 + users 5×0.25 + financial 4×0.20 + duration 5×0.20 (sub-scores 0–10 · weighted composite)

Record >40C UK heat overwhelmed cooling, forcing shutdowns at Google Cloud and Oracle London DCs — sub-scores ESTIMATED from public impact reporting, pending deep research.



## Sequence of events (SOE)




- 2022-07-19 (daytime, UK) TRIGGER UK ambient air reaches an all-time national record of 40.3C (104.5F); London experiences its first-ever day above 40C, driving cooling units toward their design limits.
- 2022-07-19 06:33 US/Pacific (13:33 UTC) TRIGGER Google incident begins: a cooling-related failure in one building hosting zone europe-west2-a; The Register (2022-08-01) reported this as a simultaneous failure of multiple redundant cooling systems under record ambient.
- 2022-07-19 (post-06:33 PDT) DETECTION Data-centre environmental/BMS temperature monitoring (NOT fire/smoke detection - no combustion) registers loss of cooling; the building could not maintain a safe operating temperature. No fire alarm - a thermal, not fire, condition.
- 2022-07-19 (immediately after detection) MITIGATION Protective thermal load-shed (de-energisation analogue): Google powers down part of the zone and limits preemptible launches to prevent machine damage. NO fire suppression discharged - no gaseous/water-mist/sprinkler activation, because there was no fire.
- 2022-07-19 IMPACT Compute Engine terminates VMs in the impacted datacenter - a small set per the public status page; ~35% of europe-west2-a VMs per The Register's report of Google's fuller incident report.
- 2022-07-19 CASCADE Recovery-procedure error widens blast radius: engineers inadvertently modify traffic routing for internal services to avoid all three europe-west2 zones rather than just the impacted europe-west2-a.
- 2022-07-19 ~16:15 UTC (~09:15 US/Pacific) DETECTION Google publicly acknowledges the fault: 'There has been a cooling-related failure in one of our buildings that hosts zone europe-west2-a for region europe-west2.'
- 2022-07-19 (UK afternoon) TRIGGER Oracle UK South (London): a subset of cooling infrastructure experiences an issue as a result of unseasonal temperatures - a second, independent London campus hit by the same heat event.
- 2022-07-19 16:38 UTC DETECTION Oracle acknowledges the cooling problem at its UK South (London) data centre.
- 2022-07-19 (after acknowledgement) MITIGATION Oracle protective power-down: identifying 'service infrastructure that can be safely powered down to prevent additional hardware failures' - thermal load-shed, not fire response.
- 2022-07-19 (throughout) IMPACT NEGATIVE FORENSICS - no personnel evacuation reported (equipment-protection shutdown, not a life-safety event) and no emergency-services / fire-brigade call or arrival is reported; response was operator engineering teams restoring cooling and rebuilding capacity.
- 2022-07-19 (afternoon, per The Register) RECOVERY Google cooling reported restored (~14:13 US/Pacific per The Register 2022-08-01) and capacity rebuild begins in europe-west2-a.
- 2022-07-19 20:43 US/Pacific (03:43 UTC 20 Jul) RESTORED Google: 'the issue has been resolved for all affected users as of Tuesday, 2022-07-19 20:43 US/Pacific' (~14h10m from 06:33 start), though some storage issues persist requiring support contact.
- 2022-07-20 (recovery update) IMPACT Storage long-tail: a small number of HDD-backed Persistent Disk volumes still exhibit IO errors, with a small percentage of replicated PDs running in single-redundant mode - genuine media damage from the thermal event/abrupt power-down.
- 2022-07-20 ~03:57 UTC (per The Register follow-up) RECOVERY Oracle data-centre cooling infrastructure reported restored and temperatures returned to normal operating levels.
- 2022-07-20 21:20 US/Pacific RESTORED Google official incident window closes. Status-page window: began 2022-07-19 06:33, ended 2022-07-20 21:20 US/Pacific (~38h47m to full closure); the extra tail beyond the 20:43 Jul 19 'resolved for all users' mark was storage remediation.



## Root cause

 SPECIFIC MECHANISM (Google, europe-west2-a, London): The proximate cause was a cooling-capacity collapse in one building hosting zone europe-west2-a on the UK's hottest day on record. Google's PUBLIC incident report (status.cloud.google.com, incident XVq5om2XEDSqLtJZUvcH) states there was "a cooling related failure in one of our buildings that hosts zone europe-west2-a for region europe-west2." The Register's 2022-08-01 reporting of Google's fuller (customer-facing) incident report characterised the mechanism more sharply — a simultaneous failure of multiple, redundant cooling systems combined with the extraordinarily high outside temperature such that the building "could not maintain a safe operating temperature." NOTE (verification): this stronger "simultaneous / multiple redundant systems" wording appears in The Register's 2022-08-01 write-up and NOT in the public status page (which says only "a cooling related failure"); it is retained as attributed reporting, not re-verified verbatim in this pass. When cooling capacity collapsed, Compute Engine executed a protective thermal load-shed and Google "powered down part of the zone" to prevent machine damage (The Register, 2022-07-19). The Register (2022-08-01) reported ~35% of europe-west2-a's VMs were terminated; the public status page confirms only "abnormal VM terminations for a small set."

LATENT ROOT — DESIGN / REDUNDANCY MARGIN: The pairing "simultaneous" + "redundant" is the tell of a latent design defect — genuine N+1/N+2 redundancy should not permit two backup-capable units to fail at effectively the same moment, which points to a common-mode driver (shared record ambient) or a single point of failure. Trade analysis (The Register, 2022-08-22, citing Tech Monitor) framed the units as failing when "required to operate above their design limits," i.e. a climate-resilience / design-margin gap: the plant lacked head-room for a 40°C day. The UK reached an all-time record 40.3°C (104.5°F) on 2022-07-19 (The Register, 2022-07-19). CAVEAT: the "two cooler units above design limits," "single point of failure," and Equinix worst-case-factory-test contrast originate in trade reporting (Tech Monitor / The Register Aug 22) that could not be independently re-fetched this pass; they are inference/analysis, not operator-disclosed fact.

MAINTENANCE / INSPECTION / TESTING LAPSE: NONE EVIDENCED in any public source. Neither Google's report nor Oracle's status notes attribute the failure to deferred maintenance, a botched service, an untested standby chiller , or a work-procedure error. The disclosed cause is environmental (record ambient) plus a cooling-system failure. Disclosed-uncertainty point: the record is silent on whether the redundant units had ever been function-tested under near-design ambient, and equipment specifics (chiller/CRAC/CRAH make, model, age, refrigerant chemistry; whether free-cooling economisers or mechanical DX/chilled-water plant failed) were NOT disclosed by either operator for either site.

ORACLE (UK South, London): Same climate trigger, less detail. "As a result of unseasonal temperatures in the region, a subset of cooling infrastructure within the UK South (London) Data Centre has experienced an issue" (Oracle status, via The Register 2022-07-19), forcing a protective power-down of "service infrastructure that can be safely powered down to prevent additional hardware failures." Oracle named no equipment, age, refrigerant, or maintenance history.


## Contributing factors



- RECORD AMBIENT / CLIMATE FORCING: The UK hit an all-time record 40.3C (104.5F) on 2022-07-19 - London's first day ever above 40C - pushing cooling units to and beyond their rated design envelope (The Register, 2022-07-19; design-limit framing via Tech Monitor/The Register, 2022-08-22, attributed-not-re-verified).
- DESIGN-MARGIN / WORST-CASE ENVELOPE SET TOO LOW: The plant appears to have lacked head-room for a 40C day; trade analysis contrasts operators that design and factory-test cooling 'for worst-case conditions' with the failed London plant, implying its worst-case design temperature trailed the emerging climate reality (The Register, 2022-08-22, trade analysis - not operator-confirmed).
- REDUNDANCY THAT DID NOT DELIVER (suspected common-mode / single point of failure): Google's fuller report (via The Register, 2022-08-01) described a simultaneous failure of multiple redundant cooling systems; simultaneity of 'redundant' units implies a shared driver (record ambient) or single point of failure rather than independent random failure.
- SELF-ADMITTED OPERATIONAL / RECOVERY-PROCEDURE ERROR: Engineers inadvertently modified traffic routing for internal services to avoid all three europe-west2 zones rather than just the impacted europe-west2-a, enlarging the blast radius beyond the physically affected zone (The Register, 2022-08-01; not on public status page).
- NO MAINTENANCE/INSPECTION LAPSE EVIDENCED, BUT TEST-UNDER-LOAD UNVERIFIED: No source attributes the failure to deferred maintenance or a botched service; however, the record is silent on whether the redundant units had ever been function-tested under near-design high ambient - an unverified resilience gap (disclosed uncertainty).
- SIMULTANEOUS TWO-OPERATOR EXPOSURE: Both Google (europe-west2-a) and Oracle (UK South) cooling plant failed the same day under the same heat event, indicating a regional/industry design-assumption gap rather than a single-site defect (The Register, 2022-07-19).
- ABRUPT DE-ENERGISATION AS A DAMAGE SOURCE: The protective emergency power-down itself contributed to lasting harm - replicated Persistent Disks left in single-redundant mode and HDD-backed volumes exhibiting IO errors (Google status page, 2022-07-19/20).



## Correction of errors (COE)



- Raise cooling-plant worst-case design ambient and factory-test to it (climate-resilience uplift for UK/comparable sites) Google DC facilities / engineering · Inferred remediation - not publicly confirmed by operator
- Add guardrails so zone-scoped traffic-routing mitigations cannot be applied region-wide (blast-radius containment) Google SRE / networking · Improvement identified in incident report per The Register - public commitment not independently confirmed
- Function-test redundant cooling units under near-design high ambient; verify economiser/chiller changeover at design-max Google & Oracle facilities · Not evidenced in any public source (recommended)
- Restore Persistent Disk redundancy and remediate HDD-backed volumes exhibiting IO errors Google storage / Compute Engine · In progress at report time per public status page
- Publish equipment/plant type and maintenance-test history to enable independent post-incident learning Google & Oracle · Not done - disclosure gap



## Lessons learnt



- CLIMATE HAS MOVED THE DESIGN TAIL: 'Once-in-a-lifetime' ambient is now design-relevant; cooling worst-case envelopes calibrated on historical UK climate under-provision for 40C+ days and must be revised upward.
- 'REDUNDANT' IS NOT 'INDEPENDENT': N+1/N+2 duplication provides no protection when all units share the same failure driver (record ambient); redundancy must be diverse and common-mode-analysed, not merely duplicated.
- BLAST RADIUS IS OFTEN OPERATIONAL, NOT PHYSICAL: The largest widening of customer impact came from a human failover-tooling error (region-wide reroute), not the cooling failure itself - recovery-tooling discipline matters as much as the plant.
- EMERGENCY DE-ENERGISATION HAS ITS OWN COST: Protective thermal shutdown left HDD-backed Persistent Disks with IO errors and replicated PDs single-redundant - the 'safe' action still damaged data durability.
- MULTI-OPERATOR SAME-DAY FAILURE IS AN INDUSTRY SIGNAL: Two independent London operators failing on the same heat event points to a shared design-assumption gap across the sector, not an isolated site defect.
- DISCLOSURE WAS PARTIAL: Neither operator released equipment make/model/age, refrigerant, plant type, or maintenance/test history - limiting external learning and independent verification.



## Improvements & remediation



- DESIGN HEAD-ROOM: Raise the cooling-plant worst-case design ambient and factory-test plant to it, so cooling retains capacity on 40C+ days rather than being 'required to operate above design limits'; UK worst-case envelopes set on historical climate are now obsolete.
- REDUNDANCY DIVERSITY (Safety-critical): Audit London (and comparable) plant for common-mode failure paths and single points of failure so that nominally 'redundant' units cannot be defeated simultaneously by a shared driver such as record ambient; add independent/diverse cooling paths, not just duplicated identical units.
- MAINTENANCE / FUNCTION-TESTING: Institute periodic function-testing of standby and redundant cooling units under near-design HIGH-ambient load (not only cool-day proof runs); verify chiller/economiser changeover and setpoints hold at design-max wet-bulb, and log test-under-load results.
- THERMAL-PROTECTION SAFETY RUNBOOK: Formalise a graceful, staged thermal load-shed runbook (migrate/drain workloads before hard VM termination where time permits) and validate BMS high-temperature alarm thresholds and shutdown setpoints to buy migration time and reduce abrupt-power-down data damage.
- RECOVERY-TOOLING GUARDRAILS: Add blast-radius containment to traffic-routing/failover tooling so a zone-scoped mitigation cannot be inadvertently applied region-wide (the europe-west2 all-three-zone reroute error).
- STORAGE DURABILITY: Harden Persistent Disk against abrupt de-energisation so emergency shutdown does not leave replicated volumes single-redundant or HDD-backed volumes with IO errors; prioritise redundancy-restore automation post-event.
- CUSTOMER RESILIENCE GUIDANCE: Reinforce multi-zone/multi-region architecture guidance, treating a single zone/building as a failure domain that can be lost to a facility-level thermal event.



## Comprehensive analysis

### What actually happened - and what did not

On 2022-07-19, the UK's hottest day on record (40.3C), cooling failed at two independent London cloud campuses - Google's europe-west2-a and Oracle's UK South. This was a thermal cooling-capacity collapse, not a fire. There was no ignition, no combustion, no smoke/heat detection, no suppression discharge, no evacuation, and no emergency-services response reported by any source. The correct analogues are environmental/BMS temperature monitoring in place of fire detection, and deliberate thermal load-shedding / de-energisation in place of fire suppression. Google confirmed 'a cooling related failure in one of our buildings that hosts zone europe-west2-a', and 'powered down part of the zone' to prevent machine damage.

### The latent root: design margin versus a changing climate

The units were, per trade reporting, 'required to operate above their design limits' - a design-margin gap rather than a maintenance failure. The plant's worst-case ambient envelope appears to have been set below the emerging UK climate reality; London had never before exceeded 40C. This reframes the event from an equipment fault to a climate-resilience shortfall: cooling designed and factory-tested for historical worst-case conditions is now under-provisioned. (The 'above design limits' framing is trade analysis via Tech Monitor/The Register and was not operator-confirmed or re-verified this pass.)

### Redundancy that did not deliver

Google's fuller report (via The Register, 2022-08-01) described a simultaneous failure of multiple redundant cooling systems. Simultaneity among 'redundant' units is the tell of a common-mode driver - here the shared record ambient - or a single point of failure . Genuine N+1/N+2 redundancy should not permit backup-capable units to fail together; that they did indicates the redundancy was duplicated rather than diverse and independent. This is the single most important engineering lesson of the event.

### Self-inflicted blast radius: the failover-tooling error

The physical impact was confined to one building/hall of europe-west2-a (europe-west2-b and -c were explicitly unaffected for VMs). The damaging secondary spread was operational: engineers inadvertently rerouted internal-service traffic away from all three europe-west2 zones rather than just the impacted one, widening customer impact. This procedural error - not the cooling failure - drove much of the customer-visible blast radius , underscoring recovery-tooling discipline. (Reported by The Register; not on the public status page.)

### Storage long-tail and the cost of emergency shutdown

Protective de-energisation is not free. Google's status page confirms 'a small percentage of replicated Persistent Disk devices are now running in single redundant mode' and 'a small number of HDD backed Persistent Disk volumes are still experiencing impact and will exhibit IO errors.' The abrupt power-down inflicted genuine storage-media damage and left durability degraded, extending the official incident window (06:33 Jul 19 to 21:20 Jul 20 US/Pacific) well past the 'resolved for all users' mark at 20:43 Jul 19.

### Two operators, one heat event, and the disclosure gap

Both Google and Oracle cooling plant failed the same day under the same heat - a sector-level design-assumption signal, not a one-off. Yet disclosure was thin: neither operator released equipment make/model/age, refrigerant chemistry, plant type (free-cooling economiser vs mechanical DX/chilled-water), maintenance/test history, MW lost, rack counts, or cost. No maintenance or inspection lapse is evidenced anywhere; equally, whether the redundant units had ever been function-tested under near-design ambient is unknown. These remain disclosed-uncertainty points, not findings.



## Technical deep-dive

 This was a thermal-overload / cooling-capacity-collapse event at two independent London cloud campuses on the UK's hottest day on record — NOT a fire. Every fire-forensic axis (ignition, detection-of-combustion, suppression discharge, evacuation, emergency-services response) is therefore a documented NEGATIVE, and the correct analogues are environmental/BMS temperature monitoring in place of smoke/heat detection, and deliberate thermal load-shedding / de-energisation in place of fire suppression.

FAILURE CHAIN (Google europe-west2-a): (1) Ambient forcing — record 40.3°C outside air (The Register, 2022-07-19) pushed mechanical cooling toward/above rated design limits. (2) Cooling failure — a cooling-related failure in the building hosting europe-west2-a (public status page); The Register (2022-08-01) reported this as a simultaneous failure of multiple redundant cooling systems, implying a common-mode driver or single point of failure so that intended redundancy did not deliver. (3) Sensed condition — data-centre environmental/BMS temperature monitoring registered rising hall temperature (NOT fire/smoke detection; no combustion). (4) Protective action — Google "powered down part of the zone" and limited preemptible launches "to prevent machine damage" (status page / The Register). This is thermal load-shedding to prevent uncontrolled hardware/thermal damage — the physical analogue of de-energisation, NOT fire suppression. No gaseous, water-mist, or sprinkler system was discharged, because there was no fire.

BLAST-RADIUS AMPLIFICATION (reported operational error): The physical "spread" was purely thermal and confined to the affected building/hall of europe-west2-a (europe-west2-b and -c were explicitly not impacted for VMs — status page). The Register (2022-08-01) reported the damaging SECONDARY spread was operational: engineers inadvertently modified traffic routing for internal services to avoid all three europe-west2 zones rather than just europe-west2-a, widening customer impact. This traffic-routing detail is not on the public status page and is retained as attributed reporting; it is a procedural (not maintenance) fault and a key recovery-tooling lesson.

RECOVERY & LONG-TAIL DAMAGE: Google confirmed "the issue has been resolved for all affected users as of Tuesday, 2022-07-19 20:43 US/Pacific," ~14h10m after the 06:33 US/Pacific start; the official incident window on the status page runs 2022-07-19 06:33 to 2022-07-20 21:20 US/Pacific (~38h47m to full closure), the extra tail driven by storage. NOTE: The Register's precise "18h23m primary / 35h15m long-tail" figures could not be verified and do not reconcile with the public window, so status-page-derived figures are used instead. Genuine media damage is confirmed on the status page: "A small percentage of replicated Persistent Disk devices are now running in single redundant mode," and later "a small number of HDD backed Persistent Disk volumes are still experiencing impact and will exhibit IO errors" — attributable to the thermal event and abrupt power-down. Oracle reported (per The Register follow-up, not re-verified this pass) cooling restored and temperatures normal by ~03:57 UTC 20 Jul, with a subset of Oracle Integration Cloud still impacted afterward.

EVIDENCE GAPS (disclosed uncertainty): No equipment make/model/age/refrigerant chemistry was released for either operator; neither stated whether economiser/free-cooling or mechanical DX/chilled-water plant failed; no maintenance/test history was published; no MW-lost, rack-count, coolant-flow, or dollar-cost figures were disclosed. No fire, no evacuation, no emergency-services response was reported by any source.

# NIRS Daejeon Government Data Center: UPS Lithium-Ion Battery Fire During Relocation Work


 National Information Resources Service (NIRS)
 2025-09-26
 10h 0m core impact
 Fire Power


On the evening of 26 September 2025, a lithium-ion UPS battery that had been disconnected in order to be relocated to the basement of the NIRS Daejeon government data center entered thermal runaway and exploded in a server room, igniting a fire that took roughly ten hours to extinguish. When the fire broke out, all 647 government IT systems at the Daejeon headquarters were taken offline (96 of them directly destroyed, the rest shut down as a precautionary safety measure). Core national services including digital IDs, Korea Post postal banking, emergency GPS tracking, courts and tax were paralyzed, and all documents on the G-Drive cloud used by up to 30 ministries and nearly 191,000 employees were permanently lost because the repository was not backed up externally. Recovery reached 70.5 percent by 24 October and later exceeded 95 percent; the NIRS chief and three other officials were booked for causing the fire through on-duty negligence, the chief was relieved of duty, and Daejeon police raided NIRS.

- 2025-09-26 night MITIGATION NIRS cuts power to all 647 Daejeon systems — protective mass shutdown as the room's HVAC/CRAC (항온항습장치) is lost, risking server overheating

- 2025-09-27 ~18:30 KST RECOVERY Fire reportedly fully extinguished ~22 hours after ignition, following repeated re-ignition characteristic of thermal runaway (press-derived secondary)

## Root cause

 At approximately 20:20 KST on 2025-09-26 a fire broke out in the fifth-floor UPS room of the National Information Resources Service (NIRS) headquarters in Yuseong-gu, Daejeon, during work to physically relocate lithium-ion UPS batteries. Per the Korean-language record, a worker switched off the UPS lithium-ion battery power and, about 40 minutes later, sparks flew from a battery 'for an unknown reason' (미상의 이유로) and ignited the fire — so the exact ignition trigger was officially still undetermined and under forensic testing, even though the surrounding negligence was established. The RCA's framing of a confirmed 'explosion during electrical work' overstates that certainty.

Korean National Police investigators concluded the relocation was performed on batteries that were neither electrically isolated nor made energetically safe to handle, and filed professional-negligence charges. Two conditions compounded. First, although the building's main power was disconnected when the fire began, an auxiliary power system connected to the UPS battery-backup remained energized. Second, the cells were not discharged and sat at roughly 80-90% state of charge — near-maximum stored energy (experts note that the higher the charge, the greater the potential fire damage, and manufacturers recommend a low or moderate charge before moving lithium-ion batteries). Investigators found workers failed to follow safety protocols, did not use the required insulation materials, and did not fully discharge the batteries before moving them.

Human and procedural safeguards were absent: the staff were not qualified for the job and had no battery-relocation experience; the battery manufacturers were deliberately excluded to cut costs; and the work had been illegally subcontracted — the two firms that won the tender handed it to three other businesses in breach of Korean law, with the two primary contractors falsifying employment records to make the crews appear to be their own staff.

Consequences were severe because recovery redundancy was inadequate at the data layer. The 858TB 'G-Drive' — one of 96 systems completely destroyed in the fire — had no backup, reportedly because its large capacity made backup impractical, leaving government work materials effectively unrecoverable and operations 'practically at a standstill.' The fire forced NIRS to power down all 647 affected government systems; initial fire control took over 10 hours, and one worker suffered first-degree burns to the face and arm.

Five people were charged with professional negligence resulting in fire — one NIRS official, one project-management-firm worker, and three construction-company employees — with charges reported in late October 2025. Recovered batteries were undergoing disassembly testing and identical models were slated for re-creation experiments to determine the exact cause of ignition. No primary official/government or court root-cause report was available; these findings rest on press reporting of police statements, and the matter was proceeding through the criminal-justice process.

Official confirmation. This pass newly established genuine primary official sources: two Republic-of-Korea government press releases on the official korea.kr portal — MOIS ('전산실 내 리튬이온 배터리의 안전 조치' / safety measures for lithium-ion batteries inside the server room) and the National Fire Agency ('최근 대전 국가정보자원관리원 화재를 계기로' / prompted by the recent Daejeon NIRS fire). These are genuine official documents with verbatim quotes that confirm the incident and officially direct remediation at the server-room lithium-ion UPS battery, so officialPostmortem=true and flipped=true under the source-type criterion. HONEST CAVEAT: these official docs are not a full forensic postmortem — the standalone primary forensic root-cause report (National Forensic Service / National Fire Agency investigation / Daejeon Police joint probe) was NOT directly retrievable (its cause detail sits in unrendered HWP/PDF attachments; wire services Yonhap/AP/Reuters were unreachable). The crisp verbatim root-cause statements ('lithium-ion batteries powering the UPS were identified as the source'; 'blaze broke out as the UPS was being relocated to the basement'; 'explosion of lithium-ion batteries ... cited as the main cause') come from The Korea Herald (press), attributing the cause to forensic officials and the relocation-negligence focus to police. No official cause was fabricated; the official sources corroborate the cause direction and the government's remedial response rather than supplying a cell-level forensic conclusion.


## Contributing factors



- Unqualified, inexperienced personnel performing the Li-ion relocation: police reportedly found the crew had no experience with large-scale battery relocations and deemed them unqualified (Anadolu, press-derived, not re-verified at review).
- Illegal subcontracting of the relocation work reportedly broke the qualification/accountability chain (Anadolu, press-derived).
- Safety protocol not followed during disconnection — plausibly disconnecting wiring before the pack was fully de-energised, producing an arc/voltage spike; ko.wikipedia (verified) labels the spark cause 'unknown,' and the arc hypothesis is secondary (breached.company).
- Aged asset kept in service and physically relocated rather than retired: reported as an LG Energy Solution bank installed August 2014, ~11 years old and past ~10-year recommended life (breached.company, single-source secondary, unverified at review).
- No battery backup for the ~858 TB G-Drive ('couldn't have a backup system due to its large capacity') — a disaster-recovery governance failure that converted a contained fire into permanent data loss for ~125,000 officials (Anadolu/DCD, press-derived).
- Physical siting of a volatile Li-ion bank close to production servers with inadequate fire separation, exposing adjacent racks to runaway heat and smoke (breached.company, secondary).
- Suppression regime mismatched to chemistry: server-hall water-cautious firefighting could not arrest a self-oxidising Li-ion runaway, driving the verified >10h initial knockdown (ko.wikipedia).
- Loss of HVAC/CRAC (항온항습장치) forced a protective mass power-down of 647 systems, widening the outage well beyond the fire's footprint (ko.wikipedia, verified).
- No disclosed battery-level off-gas/thermal-runaway early-warning detection; the event was human-noticed at ~20:15 rather than caught at cell venting (ko.wikipedia, verified).



## Correction of errors (COE)



- Retire and safely dispose of all UPS lithium-ion battery banks at/before end of recommended service life; ban physical relocation of past-life packs; require certified crews and verified full de-energisation before any disconnection. NIRS facilities / MOIS Digital Government · Proposed
- Provision real backup and geographically separate disaster recovery for all critical government stores including G-Drive, removing the 'too large to back up' exemption. MOIS / NIRS DR governance · Proposed
- Install battery-level off-gas and thermal-runaway early-warning detection and rated fire separation between Li-ion energy storage and production server halls. NIRS facilities engineering · Proposed
- Prohibit illegal subcontracting on critical-infrastructure work; enforce contractor qualification verification and safety-protocol sign-off for energy-storage handling. MOIS procurement / safety · Proposed
- Adopt Li-ion-appropriate fire response doctrine (immersion/copious-water cooling capability) and pre-plan power/cooling failure domains to bound outage blast radius. NIRS operations / local fire authority · Proposed
- Complete formal cause investigation and publish findings; resolve the 5 negligence charges through the courts. Korean National Police / prosecutors · In progress (press-reported)



## Lessons learnt



- A single-rack lithium-ion event defines its blast radius through shared power and cooling, not flame footprint: the 647-system outage came from the deliberate mass power-down and lost HVAC/CRAC as much as from the fire itself (ko.wikipedia, verified).
- Server-hall fire doctrine is incompatible with Li-ion chemistry: water-cautious tactics could not arrest a self-oxidising runaway, producing the verified >10h initial knockdown (ko.wikipedia) and reportedly ~22h to full out with repeated re-ignition (breached.company). The one effective tactic — copious water/immersion cooling — is the one the room's mission forbids.
- 'Too big to back up' is a decision, not a fact: ~858 TB was reportedly lost solely because G-Drive had no backup 'due to its large capacity' (Anadolu/DCD). Storage cost is always cheaper than total sovereign data loss.
- A passed safety inspection is not proof of battery health: a reportedly passed June 2025 inspection preceded catastrophic runaway (breached.company); pass/fail inspection without cell-level off-gas/impedance/thermal diagnostics gives false assurance.
- Human factors dominate: the fire is attributed to a disconnection during relocation with the ignition officially 'unknown' (ko.wikipedia) and police reportedly citing unqualified crew and illegal subcontracting (Anadolu) — governance of who touches energy storage matters as much as the hardware.
- Cascade risk extends beyond the fire: recovery pressure was severe enough that an official overseeing restoration reportedly died amid overwork concerns (techspot) — recovery staffing and welfare must be planned, not improvised.



## Improvements & remediation



- Mandate hazardous-work permits, verified de-energization, thermal monitoring and physical isolation for all lithium-ion battery relocation and decommissioning, removing live server rooms from the work zone.
- Relocate lithium-ion UPS energy storage into dedicated fire-rated battery rooms with early-warning gas/thermal detection and battery-appropriate suppression, separated from IT space.
- Provision isolated, tested, recoverable backups and cross-site replication for shared government cloud repositories so no single fire can cause permanent multi-ministry data loss.
- Distribute and geo-replicate critical national services across multiple facilities/availability zones to eliminate single-facility, single-event nationwide paralysis.
- Compartmentalize and fault-isolate the facility (fire zoning, independent power and cooling per hall) so that a fire in one room does not require a precautionary shutdown of the entire co-located estate.
- Institutionalize a pre-defined, drilled restoration runbook with priority tiers (Grade-1 services, cooling-first sequencing) and transparent progress reporting.



## Comprehensive analysis

### What happened (verified core)

On the evening of 2025-09-26, during relocation work on a UPS lithium-ion battery in the 5th-floor server/UPS room of the NIRS Daejeon government data center, a worker switched the battery power off and about 40 minutes later, at ~20:20 KST, sparks flew from the battery 'for an unknown reason' and a fire broke out (ko.wikipedia, verified verbatim). A first report came at ~20:15. NIRS powered off all 647 Daejeon systems as the room's HVAC/CRAC failed, and roughly 96 government online services were interrupted. Water suppression was constrained by fear of destroying the data-storage equipment, so initial knockdown took over 10 hours. One worker suffered 1st-degree burns.

### Why it became a disaster (governance amplifiers)

The physical fire was contained to a room, but the impact was national. Press reporting (Anadolu/DCD, not re-verifiable at review) states the ~858 TB G-Drive store — data for ~125,000 officials — had no backup 'due to its large capacity,' making its loss permanent, while other destroyed systems were recoverable. Police reportedly charged five people (an NIRS official, a PM-firm employee, three construction workers) with professional negligence, citing an unqualified, inexperienced crew and illegal subcontracting. The disaster scale was manufactured by DR governance, contractor governance, and asset-lifecycle failures, not by the battery alone.

### The Li-ion suppression conflict

Lithium-ion thermal runaway is self-oxidising, so clean-agent and water-cautious server-hall firefighting cannot arrest it, and it propagates cell-to-cell. The only reliable tactic — immersion/copious-water cooling — is precisely what a server room forbids to protect equipment. This is the unresolved doctrinal conflict the incident exposes: the verified >10h knockdown (ko.wikipedia) and reportedly ~22h full-out with repeated re-ignition (breached.company, secondary) are the direct symptom. No battery-level off-gas or thermal-runaway early warning was disclosed; the fire was human-noticed, not caught at cell venting.

### Sourcing and confidence

High-confidence, verified facts (ko.wikipedia, re-fetched at review): ignition ~20:20 with unknown spark cause, first report ~20:15, worker powered off battery ~40 min prior, 647 systems shut, HVAC/CRAC loss, water-suppression difficulty, >10h knockdown, ~96 services interrupted, 1 worker 1st-degree burns, presumed UPS lithium-battery cause. Press-derived and NOT re-verifiable at review (fetch 403/404, search budget exhausted): 858 TB, no-backup rationale, ~125,000 officials, 5 negligence charges, restoration %, and all breached.company technical specifics (LG Energy Solution, 384 modules, Aug-2014 install, ~60 cm siting, >160°C, ~22h, ~101 firefighters, June-2025 inspection). These are retained as attributed, hedged secondary claims, not established fact.



## Technical deep-dive

 The event is a textbook demonstration of why lithium-ion energy storage in a server hall defeats the fire-protection assumptions data centers are built on. A conventional server-hall fire regime — clean-agent (inert gas or chemical clean agent) plus cautious or prohibited water application to protect equipment — is designed for combustion that needs external oxygen. A Li-ion cell in thermal runaway is self-oxidising: the decomposing cathode liberates oxygen internally, so smothering agents cannot starve it, and the reaction propagates cell-to-cell as each venting cell heats its neighbours. With the pack reported at 384 modules, once one cell failed during disconnection the runaway chained across the bank (breached.company, secondary). This is why the fire "reignited repeatedly" and why full extinguishment reportedly took ~22 hours after ignition, with initial knockdown alone taking over 10 hours — the >10h figure is verified in ko.wikipedia ("초진까지 10시간 이상이 소요되었다"), while the ~22h full-out and >160°C peak are press-derived secondary.

The suppression dilemma is the central operational lesson. The room's fixed suppression did not arrest the event. ko.wikipedia (verified) states water-based firefighting was difficult because of concern over damaging the data-storage equipment, driving the >10-hour initial knockdown. But gas/clean agent cannot quench a self-oxidising runaway, and cautious water cannot rapidly cool cascading modules. The only reliable Li-ion tactic — total immersion / copious water cooling — was the one tactic the room's mission forbade. That unresolved conflict is what this incident exposes.

The second dynamic is the de-energisation cascade. NIRS cut power to all 647 Daejeon systems ("647개 시스템"), partly a protective shutdown because the fire and response knocked out the room's HVAC/CRAC (항온항습장치); without cooling and dehumidification, running servers would overheat (ko.wikipedia, verified). So the outage was driven as much by the deliberate mass power-down and lost cooling as by flame — in a dense DC the blast radius of a single-rack event is defined by shared power and cooling topology, not the fire's physical footprint. Detection specifics (VESDA/aspirating, spot smoke/heat, or battery off-gas detection) and any automated-alarm time are NOT disclosed in any source; what is documented is a human-noticed first report at ~20:15 KST and ignition at ~20:20 (ko.wikipedia). No source indicates any battery-level gas or thermal-runaway early-warning system caught cell venting before flame — a detection gap that, for Li-ion, is the difference between a vented cell and a multi-hour fire.

# NorthC Almere Data Center Fire: A Compartment Blaze That Took Out the Facility Power Plant and Rippled Across Dutch Public Services


 NorthC Datacenters
 2026-05-07
 144h 0m core impact
 Fire Power


On 7 May 2026 (around 08:45 local time) a fire broke out in a rear technical compartment of NorthC's Almere data center (Rondebeltweg) that houses power infrastructure. No servers or data carriers caught fire, but the blaze burned part of the facility's power supply and the site lost power entirely — the compute survived, yet everything went dark, and NorthC ultimately had to rebuild the power plant with new transformers and UPS. (Published reporting says only that 'part of the power supply burnt down'; that BOTH the normal and standby feeds were lost is an engineering inference from the total, multi-day power loss and the full rebuild, not an official finding.) Because multiple Dutch organizations host critical systems there, the outage cascaded outward: Utrecht University, Statistics Netherlands (CBS), public-transport operator Transdev, a regional water board, research-ICT provider Surf, IBM Cloud's Amsterdam 03, and numerous GP practices all lost service. The fire was scaled down to GRIP 1 at 20:50 that evening and to GRIP 0 with the building partially released to NorthC teams at 00:35 on 8 May, kicking off a phased restoration estimated at up to 72 hours. Temporary redundant power and cooling were activated on 13 May, roughly a week after the fire. Grid power came back building-by-building over the following weeks, with Building 1's full utility-plus-standby topology targeted for 17 July 2026. The root cause remains officially undetermined; a draft cause report was only expected at end-September 2026 because the fire-damaged structure had to be secured first.

## Root cause

 SPECIFIC IGNITION SOURCE — NOT PUBLICLY DISCLOSED (investigation open). No primary or press source names the equipment that ignited: no make, model, age, or chemistry, and no failure mechanism. On day one NorthC stated plainly that nothing was yet known about the cause. NorthC commissioned an independent expert investigation, but forensic work could only begin after the severely damaged, unstable structure was secured (a demolition/investigation window of 27 July–7 August 2026), and NorthC expects only a DRAFT cause report by end of September 2026. As of the reporting window the ignition source and chemistry are genuinely unknown; any specific attribution would be fabrication.

WHAT IS FIRMLY ESTABLISHED (confirmed on the official NorthC status page) is the location and the affected system class. The fire started at the rear of the building, where the technical facilities are located, inside the emergency-power / technical room of the "Almere 1" compartment, and centred on the site's power infrastructure. The consequence set narrows the field: the transformers and UPS systems in that compartment were destroyed and the emergency electrical installation was "classified as lost" (NorthC), while no IT gear was fire-damaged (DataCenterDynamics, crawl-cited). That the destroyed plant was UPS + transformers makes two failure families physically plausible — (a) a UPS energy-storage thermal event (a VRLA or Li-ion battery string entering thermal runaway ) or (b) an electrical fault in a transformer or switchgear /distribution assembly (arc flash, insulation breakdown, connection overheating). BOTH are UNCONFIRMED; no source attributes ignition to either, and this dossier asserts neither.

LATENT / SYSTEMIC ROOT (what the record supports). At the operator level the design worked as intended where it mattered for life-safety and containment: the two-compartment topology and PASSIVE fire compartmentation confined the fire to the rear power room and kept the data halls and their IT largely intact — "The fire compartmentation prevented the smoke from spreading further" and "smoke in the halls remained limited" (NorthC, verified). Where the design failed was in continuity of the affected compartment's own power train: the fire took out transformers and UPS together, i.e. primary and backup power for Almere 1 shared enough physical proximity in one technical room that a single fire destroyed the entire emergency electrical installation of that half of the site. That is a redundancy / physical-separation latent root inside Almere 1's power topology, even though inter-compartment separation (Almere 1 vs Almere 2) held.

Second — the more consequential systemic root for the outside world — the severe downstream impact was NOT caused by any NorthC fire-safety failing but by SINGLE-SITE customer architectures with no disaster-recovery failover. Transdev's regional control-centre servers had not been migrated to a backup location, so bus drivers lost communications and the in-vehicle emergency button stopped working; Utrecht University, Infomedics and the local water board carried single-site dependencies on this one facility (TNW / Computable, crawl-cited).

MAINTENANCE / INSPECTION / TESTING LATENT ROOT — NONE EVIDENCED, NOT EXONERATED. No source implicates any hot-work permit, deferred maintenance, failed test, or procedural breach at NorthC — consistent with the cause investigation still being open. Any maintenance-cause theory must be treated as unproven pending the expert report (draft due end September 2026).


## Contributing factors



- Co-location of primary and backup power in one room (Almere 1): a single fire in the rear technical room destroyed transformers AND UPS together, so the entire emergency electrical installation of that compartment was 'classified as lost' (NorthC, verified) — indicating insufficient physical separation between the power train's redundant elements within Almere 1.
- Absence (or non-disclosure) of effective automatic suppression in the affected power room: no source evidences that any gaseous / water-mist / sprinkler system discharged or held the fire, which burned ~11–12 hours and required manual firefighting until 'brand meester' at ~20:30 (Omroep Flevoland, crawl-cited). Whether a suppression system existed and failed, or was never installed, is an open gap.
- Structural fragility of the burning compartment slowed both firefighting and forensics: the room was too unstable and too damaged to send crews inside, forcing crane demolition of the facade and drone imaging (Omroep Flevoland, crawl-cited) — extending outage duration and pushing the cause investigation to a 27 July–7 August 2026 demolition/investigation window (NorthC, verified).
- Customer-side single-site architecture with no DR failover (a downstream contributor to IMPACT, not to ignition): Transdev's regional control-centre servers 'had not been migrated to a backup location' (TNW, crawl-cited), collapsing bus-driver communications and the in-vehicle emergency button; Utrecht University, Infomedics and the local water board carried single-facility dependencies.
- Maintenance / inspection / testing status is UNEVIDENCED, not exonerated: with the cause investigation open and only a draft report due end September 2026 (NorthC, verified), no maintenance, hot-work, or testing lapse has been disclosed or ruled out — the factor cannot be assessed from the public record.



## Correction of errors (COE)



- Independent expert cause investigation (ignition source, chemistry, mechanism) NorthC + independent experts · In progress — investigation/demolition window 27 Jul–7 Aug 2026; DRAFT report expected end September 2026
- Activate temporary redundant power train for Almere 1 (generators, UPS, distribution, >1 km cable) NorthC · Completed 13 May 2026
- Reconnect Almere 2 to the electricity grid NorthC · Completed 29 May 2026
- Rebuild Almere 1 emergency electrical installation (reinstall transformers + UPS) and restore to grid NorthC · Phased — initial grid connection end June; full grid operation targeted end July 2026
- Publish detection-to-alarm timeline and automatic-suppression status for the affected power room NorthC · Open / not disclosed
- Review and implement DR failover for single-site critical dependencies Tenants (Transdev, Utrecht University, Infomedics, water board) · Tenant-side — open; Utrecht University damages claim reportedly directed at KPN, not NorthC



## Lessons learnt



- Passive compartmentation is the hero of this incident — it confined an intense power-room fire and kept the data halls and IT largely intact with no injuries; sustained investment in passive fire separation pays off exactly when active systems are absent or unknown.
- Redundancy that shares a room is not redundancy — co-locating transformers and UPS in one technical space meant a single fire took out an entire compartment's power train; physical separation, not just N+1 counts, defines real resilience.
- Facility resilience does not equal customer resilience — the worst real-world harm (bus comms and the in-vehicle emergency button failing) fell on a tenant that had not replicated to a backup site; operators should actively push single-site critical customers toward DR.
- Cause timelines stretch to months when the structure is unsafe — forensics were gated by a demolition window, so a draft cause report only ~4.5 months out is a realistic expectation, not negligence; set stakeholder expectations accordingly.
- Silence on detection and suppression erodes trust — the absence of any public detail on fire detection or automatic suppression is itself a finding; transparent post-incident disclosure (once safe) is part of operational credibility.



## Improvements & remediation



- Safety (disclosure): once the expert report permits, publish the detection-to-alarm timeline and whether any automatic suppression existed in the power room, discharged, and held — the ~11–12 h manual firefight and total silence on active suppression are the single largest unexplained safety gaps in the public record.
- Design (separation): physically separate the redundant elements of each compartment's power train (transformers, UPS/battery, switchgear) into distinct fire compartments so a single fire cannot destroy both primary and backup power for one hall, as happened in Almere 1.
- Maintenance (assurance): once the cause report lands, publish the technical room's maintenance, inspection, hot-work and testing history; institute an independent thermographic/IR inspection cadence on transformers, switchgear and UPS, plus continuous battery-string health/temperature monitoring for early thermal-runaway detection.
- Customer resilience: advise/require single-site critical tenants (mobility, health, utilities such as Transdev, Utrecht University, Infomedics, the water board) to implement DR failover to a second site, since facility resilience did not prevent tenant outages.
- Emergency response: pre-plan structural-collapse firefighting access for power rooms (external attack points, pre-engineered crane/demolition access) so a compartment that becomes too unstable to enter does not extend the outage by ~11–12 hours.
- Battery chemistry: confirm and disclose the UPS battery chemistry (VRLA vs Li-ion) and, where Li-ion, deploy off-gassing/aspirating detection and battery-room-rated suppression sized for thermal runaway.



## Comprehensive analysis

### What happened

At ~08:30–08:45 on 7 May 2026 a fire broke out in the rear technical room of the 'Almere 1' compartment of NorthC's Almere data center, centred on the site's power infrastructure. Everyone was evacuated in time with no injuries. Transformers and UPS in that room were destroyed and the emergency electrical installation was 'classified as lost' (NorthC, verified). The fire brigade ordered a full shutdown and fought the blaze into the evening, with 'brand meester' reported around 20:30. The ignition source and chemistry remain publicly unknown; NorthC expects only a draft cause report by end September 2026.

### Why the data halls survived: passive containment

The load-bearing safety story is passive fire compartmentation, not active suppression. Per NorthC, 'The fire compartmentation prevented the smoke from spreading further' and 'smoke in the halls remained limited.' The two-compartment topology held between Almere 1 and Almere 2, so no IT gear was fire-damaged even as the Almere 1 power room was destroyed. No source discloses whether any automatic suppression existed in that room or discharged — a genuine gap given an ~11–12 hour manual firefight.

### The real single point of failure: a co-located power train

Inter-compartment separation worked, but within Almere 1 the primary and backup power shared one technical room closely enough that a single fire destroyed transformers and UPS together — the entire emergency electrical installation of that half of the site. This is the central latent root: redundancy defined by device counts (N+1) rather than physical fire separation collapses to a single point of failure when both elements sit in one space. Rebuild and future design should place redundant power-train elements in distinct fire compartments.

### Downstream impact was a customer-architecture failure, not a NorthC fire-safety failure

The most visible real-world harm came from single-site tenant architectures. Transdev's regional control-centre servers 'had not been migrated to a backup location' (TNW, crawl-cited), so bus-driver communications and the in-vehicle emergency button failed. Utrecht University, Infomedics and the local water board carried single-facility dependencies. Utrecht University's reported damages claim targets its telecom provider KPN, not a NorthC maintenance breach — underscoring that DR failover is a tenant responsibility the operator should actively encourage.

### What remains unknown — and why that is defensible

Three things are genuinely undisclosed: (1) the ignition source/equipment/chemistry, (2) the detection technology and first-alarm time, and (3) whether any automatic suppression existed or discharged. The cause gap is defensible: forensics could only start after an unstable structure was secured (27 Jul–7 Aug window), so a draft report ~4.5 months out is realistic. The detection/suppression gaps are less defensible as disclosure and should be closed once safe. No maintenance, hot-work, or testing lapse is evidenced — but with the investigation open, none is ruled out either.



## Technical deep-dive

 The NorthC Almere site is an 11 MW facility of roughly 26,000 sqm across two buildings, split into two functionally separate power/fire compartments referred to as "Almere 1" and "Almere 2" (11 MW / 26,000 sqm figures from DataCenterDynamics, crawl-cited and not independently re-verified this pass). The fire, at approximately 08:30–08:45 on Thursday 7 May 2026, originated in the rear technical room housing Almere 1's emergency-power plant (NorthC dates the outbreak to "around 08:45"; Omroep Flevoland/TNW report ~08:30).

Two forensic facts dominate the physics. FIRST, this was an ELECTRICAL / POWER-PLANT fire, not an IT-white-space fire: damage was concentrated around the site's power infrastructure, the transformers and UPS in the Almere 1 room were destroyed, and "the emergency electrical installation was classified as lost" (NorthC, verified), while no IT gear was fire-damaged (DCD, crawl-cited). SECOND, PASSIVE containment — not active suppression — is what saved the halls: "The fire compartmentation prevented the smoke from spreading further" and "smoke in the halls remained limited" (NorthC, verified).

Two disclosure gaps must be stated honestly. DETECTION: no source discloses the detection technology, zone, or first-alarm time. What is documented is the human outcome — the building was evacuated in time with no injuries; per CEO Alexandra Schless, "All people present were evacuated from the building in time" (NorthC, verified). ACTIVE SUPPRESSION: no source states whether any automatic suppression (gaseous/clean-agent, water-mist, sprinkler) was installed in the affected power room, whether it discharged, or why it failed to hold. This is a real gap: the fire burned into the evening and was fought manually, with "brand meester" (fire under control) reported only around 20:30 — roughly 11–12 hours after outbreak (Omroep Flevoland, crawl-cited). Firefighting was severely hampered because the compartment was too unstable and too damaged to send crews inside; facade sections were demolished with cranes for access, a drone from Brabant was flown for interior imaging, and a fire truck from Lelystad Airport assisted (Omroep Flevoland / Computable, crawl-cited).

The electrical response and recovery are the best-documented portion and are confirmed against the official NorthC status page. The fire department ordered a complete datacenter shutdown. In the undamaged half, the backup generators started automatically ("De noodstroomgeneratoren in het andere deel (Almere 2) sloegen automatisch aan," Computable, crawl-cited). Almere 1, having lost its transformers and UPS, required a full temporary power train — generators, UPS, distribution units and more than 1 km of cable — activated on 13 May (about six days post-fire; NorthC confirms "temporary power May 13"). Almere 2 was reconnected to the grid on 29 May; Almere 1 was reinstated in phases (transformers/UPS reinstalled) with initial grid connection by end June and full grid operation targeted end July 2026 (all confirmed on the NorthC page). Veiligheidsregio Flevoland ran the incident at GRIP 2 with an NL-Alert advising residents to avoid smoke, close windows/doors and disable mechanical ventilation as smoke drifted south toward 't Gooi; emergency measurements found no dangerous-substance concentrations. Reported GRIP de-escalation (GRIP 2 → GRIP 1 ~20:50 on 7 May, NL-Alert withdrawn; → GRIP 0 ~00:35 on 8 May) originates with Veiligheidsregio Flevoland / Omroep Flevoland and was not independently re-verified this pass.

# Optus Australia Nationwide Outage — Routing Change Cascade (November 8, 2023)


 Optus (Singtel)
 2023-11-08
 14h 0m core impact
 Network Software


Following a routine Singtel-network software upgrade, a large, unexpected flood of routing information exceeded preset safety limits on Optus routers, which self-isolated and cascaded into a roughly 14-hour nationwide outage of Optus mobile and internet for about 10 million Australians — disrupting triple-zero (000) emergency calls, hospitals, transport and payments.

## Sequence of events (SOE)




- 7-8 Nov 2023 (pre-onset) TRIGGER Scheduled software upgrade performed on a router at a North American node of Singtel's international peering network, the upstream infrastructure Optus's IP core depends on.
- 8 Nov 2023, ~04:05 AEDT TRIGGER The Singtel exchange upgrade caused one router to disconnect, initiating an abnormal BGP route-advertisement event toward Optus's AS4804.
- 8 Nov 2023, ~04:05 AEDT DETECTION Cloudflare telemetry for AS4804 registered the anomaly as a mass BGP spike — 'over 940,000 announcements in an hour from a node that normally makes less than 3,000 announcements per hour.'
- 8 Nov 2023, ~04:05 AEDT DETECTION Optus's Cisco PE routers registered the flood as incoming route updates crossed 'the pre-configured default threshold limits set by Cisco Systems.'
- 8 Nov 2023, ~04:05 AEDT MITIGATION Built-in threshold self-protection activated as designed: routers began tearing down BGP sessions to prevent CPU/memory exhaustion.
- 8 Nov 2023, ~04:05-04:10 AEDT CASCADE 'Approximately 90 edge provider routers disconnected as an automated protective measure against routing update overload' — a synchronized self-isolation across the PE fleet.
- 8 Nov 2023, ~04:10 AEDT CASCADE With ~90 PE routers withdrawn from BGP, Optus's IP core effectively vanished from the internet for its customers (network-layer 'de-energisation').
- 8 Nov 2023, morning IMPACT Nationwide loss of mobile and fixed service affecting 'more than 10 million people' and '400,000 businesses.'
- 8 Nov 2023, morning IMPACT Emergency Triple-Zero (000) calls failed for affected customers; exact count of failed calls not in retrievable record.
- 8 Nov 2023, 05:00-06:00 AEDT IMPACT Physical-world cascade: Melbourne's train network experienced a shutdown from 05:00 to 06:00 and about 500 train services were cancelled; hospital phone lines and EFTPOS/payment terminals were disrupted.
- 8 Nov 2023, daytime CASCADE Customers diverted to rivals: TPG/Vodafone reported a roughly four-fold activity increase and Kogan Mobile a ~400% rise in eSIM sales (press figures, not re-verified this session).
- 8 Nov 2023, daytime MITIGATION Optus publicly confirmed the outage was 'not due to a cyberattack,' focusing recovery on the routing fault.
- 8 Nov 2023, morning-afternoon RECOVERY Because tripped BGP sessions do not self-heal, engineers manually reconnected/rebooted affected routers (manual/on-site detail inferred from the recovery profile).
- 8 Nov 2023, ~11:30 AEDT RECOVERY Partial restoration reached approximately 11% of the network.
- 8 Nov 2023, ~13:00 AEDT RECOVERY Restoration advanced to approximately 88% of the network.
- 8 Nov 2023, ~evening RESTORED Full service restored after approximately 12-13 hours (some media reported up to a 14-hour outage).
- Nov 2023 (aftermath) IMPACT Singtel lost over AU$2 billion in value, a 4.8% share-price drop attributed to the outage.
- 20 Nov 2023 IMPACT Optus CEO Kelly Bayer Rosmarin resigned; a Senate public inquiry and an independent government (Bean) review were established.



## Root cause

 The proximate ignition was a scheduled software upgrade on a router at a North American node of Singtel's international peering network — the upstream infrastructure Optus's IP core depends on as a Singtel subsidiary. Per the retrievable record, "a software upgrade at a North American Singtel exchange caused one router to disconnect," and that disconnection acted as the spark: it emitted an abnormal flood of BGP routing advertisements toward Optus's autonomous system AS4804. Cloudflare telemetry (as cited by Wikipedia) recorded "over 940,000 announcements in an hour from a node that normally makes less than 3,000 announcements per hour" — roughly a 300-fold surge. (Note: some enriched sourcing named this the "STiX/Singtel Internet Exchange" fabric; the retrievable record confirms only "a North American Singtel exchange," so the specific fabric name is not established here.)

The specific vulnerable equipment was Optus's fleet of Provider Edge (PE) routers, confirmed to be Cisco Systems devices. The failure mechanism was a BGP route-limit self-protection trip: the flood caused Optus routers to "rapidly update routing tables and exceed the pre-configured default threshold limits set by Cisco Systems," and each router responded by executing the standard protective action of tearing down its BGP session to avoid CPU/memory exhaustion. "Approximately 90 edge provider routers disconnected as an automated protective measure against routing update overload." The safety mechanism performed exactly as engineered — but its activation IS the outage: by isolating themselves, the ~90 PE routers severed Optus customers from the network. The exact Cisco model, firmware and hardware age are not disclosed in the retrievable record.

The latent root causes are two change-management/configuration design lapses evidenced by the technical description. First, an upstream peering-hygiene gap: a Singtel exchange upgrade was permitted to leak a ~940,000-route flood downstream into Optus with no apparent prefix-filtering or rate-limiting to contain it — a foreseeable containment gap at the peering boundary (inferred from the mechanism, not a verbatim finding). Second, an Optus-side configuration lapse: its PE routers were left on Cisco's DEFAULT threshold ceilings rather than thresholds tuned to Optus's real route counts and headroom, so a foreseeable flood tripped a hard fail-safe (session teardown) rather than degrading gracefully. Because the identical default limit tripped near-simultaneously across ~90 PE routers, the "containment" produced a synchronized disconnection cascade rather than a firebreak. Attribution of change ownership was reportedly disputed (Singtel was reported to have refuted early causation claims; not re-verified this session). Optus expressly ruled out a cyberattack. The independent government (Bean) review and the Senate/ACMA processes were established to examine these change-management, Triple-Zero failover and recovery shortcomings; their verbatim findings were NOT directly retrievable this session (government servers returned HTTP 403 / timed out).


## Contributing factors



- Configuration/maintenance lapse on Optus PE routers: they were left on 'the pre-configured default threshold limits set by Cisco Systems' rather than thresholds tuned to Optus's real route counts, so a foreseeable flood tripped a hard fail-safe instead of degrading gracefully (Wikipedia, citing the outage account).
- Synchronized fail-safe design flaw: because the identical default limit tripped across ~90 PE routers near-simultaneously, the protective mechanism produced a fleet-wide disconnection cascade rather than isolating a single fault — the 'containment' had no firebreak (Wikipedia).
- Upstream peering-hygiene gap (inferred from mechanism): a North American Singtel exchange upgrade was allowed to propagate a ~940,000-route BGP event downstream toward AS4804 (normal

# OVHcloud SBG2 Strasbourg Data-Center Fire (10 March 2021)


 OVHcloud
 2021-03-10
 9h 27m core impact
 Fire Power


In the early hours of 10 March 2021 a fire broke out in a ground-floor energy room at OVHcloud's SBG2 facility in Strasbourg, where the site's UPS units and their lead-acid battery banks were housed. Video surveillance and the fire panel traced the initiating event to a near-simultaneous electrical fault on UPS2 and its connected batteries. With no automatic suppression system in any of the five campus buildings, and a free-cooling design that used intumescent-treated raw-wood floors and single-skin cladding to aid airflow, the fire spread through the entire structure. De-energisation was slow because there was no accessible general site cut-off, forcing the grid operator to isolate an upstream substation; current was still present in the burning building well after the cut order. SBG2 was destroyed in its entirety, four of twelve rooms in adjacent SBG1 were partially destroyed, and the SBG2–SBG3 inter-building link was impacted. Roughly 30,000 servers were lost and about 3.6 million websites went offline. There were no casualties or injuries. French investigator BEA-RI could establish the fault location but not its precise cause, leaving several hypotheses open pending a court-expert examination.
